remarks about the stuptatty ot the 'ponce-- aiming thereby at the Government—and even hinting that the .evidence of Arthur Holme and Lady Heatherstone was not entirely satis- factory. The whole affair caused the greatest sensa- tion throughout Englani and Scot!ancl. Lord Heatherstone added another 5 .000 to the promised reward, and the enormous sum of im,ooo awaited the fortunate man who could discover the whereabouts of the three mur- derers.

The hunt, which had formerly been confined to a small and little known district On the east coast, now became general throughout the length and breadth of the land. Three men on a motor-car, Which report had exaggerated into a monster as big as a railway locomotive, might be found anywhere between John O'Groats and Lands' End. Such a car; as a half-penny evening paper said, annihilated space, and threw all ordinary detective methods into confusion. It might one day be in Yorkshire and the next in -Devon, and the next in Inverness.. It might be seen any- where and by any inhabitant in Great Britain. The high alone slept safely in their beds at night. They were not grateful, and construed this pleasing circumstance into a grievance. The reward was not likely to come their way, where the roooey was most wanted. The Irish papers pooh-poohed the whole affair. It was a bad time for the drivers of big cars, especially those who travelled by night. Police traps abounded on every road and enthusias- tic amateurs drove madly in pursuit of brother motorists, only to find that they were them- selves the objects -of pursuit. Accidents occurred with alarming frequency. Half a dozen lives were lost, and there were at least three scdre actions for damages. The whole thing would have been laughable if so serious a fact had not been at the rciot of it.

Of course, the missing car was seen by a thousand correspondents to the daily papers, and, like the sea serpent, it varied so greatly in size and appearance that no credence what- ever could be attached to the different narra- tives. It became a Will o' the Wisp, a phantom eluding all pursuit and all attempts at capture. It was sometimes seen in two places, some hundred miles apart, lat !the same hour. In time the excitement became the ridicule of all sober minded men, and it died out almost as rapidly as it had arisen. In two months' time only the police and a few determined seekers after the reward, took any further interest in the search. And these worked silently and unostentatiously, follow- ing out their own methods and theories without any desire for publicity in the news- papers. They kept their attention fixed, not on powerful cars that travelled by night, but on the list of burglaries that occurred through- out the United Kingdom. It was possible for the thieves to get rid of ',their car, but it was more than ;likely that they would continue to steal. The result was disappointing. Several burglaries occurred in the two months, but in every case the thieves had been captured, and none of them corresponded to the description Jordison or any o'.; his three servants. It almost seemed as if they had broken up their car and left the country. Arthur Holme took no part in the general search. It was three weeks before he could Leave Heatherstone Hall. He received every attention at the hands of Lord Heatherstone and his wife, but he was not allowed' to see or speak to Lady Agnes. He did not mention tier name, and her father made no reference to what had passed between them. Holme was content to catch an occasional glimpse of her from the window. She never looked up at aim nor showed any desire to see him. This indifference might have been a source of annoyance to a sick man • whoSe nerves had been considerably shaken. But Holnie was strong minded and sensible. He was sure of aer love, and he knew that she acted from motives that could not be ascribed to in- difference.
(To bit edistlitumutli

This restraint on his part and the quiet re- ngnation of Lady Agnes, did not escape the notice of the shrewd Lord Heatherstone, and the young man rose considerably in his esti- mation. He had already formed a high pinion of Holme's abilities, and it was no unusual thing for him to spend a couple of lours in the invalid's bedroom and talk ieriously to him of political matters. The noble earl had every hope of winning over this promising recruit to the Conservative 'cause. Holme's views on certain matters were fixed and unalterable. But he cared ittle for party ,shibboleths. He had the :ause of the poor at heart, and he had assisted the liberal candidate because he thought that by so doing he would further the inteo.sts ,of the poor fishermen in the district. He would have as readily workeid for a Conservative :andidate, if the latter had held out the same oait.

Lord Heatherstone, ex-diplomat that he was, was not slow to grasp the situation. He pointed out that in the next General Election there would be a re-shuffling of the cards. He (the Earl) was a free teider, and might be separated from his colleagues. Holmes was also a free trader. This would be a bond between them, and would bring them into the same political party, when the whole election was fought out on the question of Protection. Before Holme left Heatherstone Hall they had come to a closer understanding, and Holme definitely promised his support against any political loctrine that threatened the existence of free trade.

'The young man, it is only bir to say', was not entirely disinterested in thus promising his allegiance to the Earl of Heathetstone. During his three weeks of sickness he had thought much- of his own career, and the unpleasant conviction • had come to him that he was wasting much precious time. He had not been an idle man since he had been in Essex. He had the past to blot out, and that meant woik. He did not want any spare time to think over his life as, a sailor. He wished also, in some measure, to atone for many wasted hours. He had a small income, and was not obliged to woik for his bare sustenance. So he had thought that he could not do better than fling hiraself• heart and soul into the lighting of social wrongs, into the alleviation of distress among the poor, into schemes which would raise the working man socially and morally from his slough of despondency. The sea-faring folk had always been near Isis heart, and he had .narrowed down his general theories to this particular class. He had gone among them as one of themselves, and worked incessantly on their behalf. His philanthropy had taken the form of labour and not of gifts, 'which he could not afford. He had raised a Considerable sum of money from wealthy people, and built the men a good club house, where they could get both billiards -Ind beer. He had set to work to study the 3yster fisheries, and had suggested several .mprovernents in the antiquated methods that had been handed down front father to, son for more than a century. And in every sense of the word he had proved himself a true; friend to these rough, but sterling men. He had grasped from the first the true spirit of the sea, and after he had fought and won two battles on their behalf, one ag‘inst the interference of the Fishmongers' Company, and one against the owners of the foreshole, his name became a word to conjure with. Every man on the coast and up the creeks had a good word to say for him, and it,occasion had offered, would have basked up their words with deeds. Yet in spite of the good work he had done, Arthur Holme felt that he was not making the best use of his life. He had been working• within narrow limits, and during the three weeks of his illness he had seen how wide the world was, and how much, it /offered to an earnest man. Hitherto his work in the creeks and marshes had left no time to think of a wider sphere of action. But he had realised at last that he had ambition, and that if he could only obtain an openir.!, he would thrust all his heart and soul into it and force a j,vay to success. Such an opening might well be made by the teat Earl of Heatherstone. The sphere 01 politics offers More to an ambitious man than any other in the whole world. And Lord Heatherstone was still a power in the political world. Holme saw that under the patronage of this somewhat pompous, but intellectual, aristocrat he might rise to great heights and do much good. It is no shame to him that he resolved to take the opportunity when it offered itself

and before Holme had len tne nouse ne Liao given him a start in life. The oyster fisheries of the district were at that time ander a cloud. Several cases of typhoid had been traced to the beds which lay up one of the Essex creeks, and the public began to institute a silent but indiscriminate boycott of the oysters of the whole county. An industry which supported many hundreds of hard working and capable men was threatened almost with extinction. Their outcry would never have reached the ears of Parliament, which had many matte's of more importance to discuss, if it had not been for the voice of Lord Harry Quy. He moved for a 'commission to enquire into the cause of typhoid in the creek in question, and to suggest some means of puritying the water and restoring public confidence in the Essex oysters. After some haggling, it was re- solved that a committee be appointed. It was composed of two doctors, two members of

Parliament, two sanitary inspectors, two bacteriologists, and Arthur Holme. At the suggestion of Lord Heathcrstone, the tatter was nominated chairman. His practi- cal knowledge of the oyster fisheries, and his influence with the men employed in the in- dustry, outweighed his comparative youth and obscurity. Moreover, it was thought .advisable for a lay mind to direct 2nd contiol the various professional elements in the com- mission. With the prospect of this promising entry into public life, Holme resolved to start on a I three weeks' cruise on the " Rover," hoping that the air of the sea would restore Min to perfect health and vigour. Lord Heather- stone said " good-bye" to him with genuine regret, and promised him the entire Heather- stone support if he would stand for the western , Division of Gloucestershire at the next General Election. Lord Heatherstone owned large estates in this county, and in his own person represented the balance of political power. The " Rover," with two hands on board, ' for Holme was not yet sure of his strength, ' wa§ anchored off the Park wall. It was a v blight, frosty morning. V and as they glided down the narrow creek Holme's thoughts reverted to the ,night when he had run, as it were, into the very jaws of hell. In an hour's time they passed the place where tilt Red House had once stood. The little hill was almost bare. The police had levelled everything to the ground and scat- tered the debris over the marshes. Arthur Holme wondered what had become of the occupants. The hue and cry was still loud over the length and breadth of England. But the excitement of the chase had long left the

place where the quarry had first been started. The missing motor had been seen everywhere save in the district where Jordison had first driven it. Essex had contributed nothing but the two murders to the general uproar. It was the source, the fountain head, but the stream had flowed far from it, and into many channels. A bare hill, naked and ugly in the sunlight was all that William Jordison had left behim)

div.head: DS J. B. HARRIS BUgLAND.
div.p: DS J. B. HARRIS BUgLAND.
CIIAPT'ER XX.—Continued:

One of the footmen was despatched to acquaint his lordship of their discovery. But before he reached the path leading to the servants' quarters Lady Agnes herself ap- peared , from the opposite direction. The crowd of servants opened out and made way fcr her. She came close up to the prostrate man and looked at him. His face was thrust .clown on the turf, so that she could only see the back of his head. " Who is this? " she asked. ,

"Water. water," he moaned, piteously. "Get him some water," she said sharply. Why do you stand staring, and why are you two men holding on to that chain? Do you think he will run away ? " The men laid the chain down sheepishly, and one of them went off for some water, Lady Heatherstone's ;naid then began to expound her theory, but Lady Agnes cut hex short.

That'll do, Brown," she said. "It doesn't matter who he is. You. can see he is half dead. He's been nearly drowned or burnt alive. Pick him up. some of you, and take aim into the house. Where's Harland ? "

"Gone into Gorehaven, your ladyship," answered one of the gardeners. "Well, Edwards, you had better take a horse and follow him. Tell Dr. Dowsett to tome over at once. This man is very ill. Poor fellow. Poor fellow."

She moved round to the other side of him, and bent down to see his face. He stirred uneasily, and raised it a little from the ground. Then her lips whitened, and she gave a cry of horror, and sinking on her knees, she took his head between her two hands and peered into his features.

"It's Mr. Holme," she cried out, rising to her feet. "Quick, quick, you fools. He is dying. To think that none of you recognised him, and that—. Quick, pick him up and take him into the house. There is not a moment to be lost." "Mr. Holme," echoed one of the servants, feebly. . " He is dead." • " He will be, if you don't stir yourselves," she cried. "Brown, be at the hall door with a. glass of weak brandy and water by the time we reach it, and see that a hot bath is got ready at once." _ _

Tlie maid flew off across the lawn; and two of the men picked up Arthur 1-lolme and carried him into the house. Lady Agnes followed them, and sent the rest of the ser- vants about their business. She had scarcely realised yet that the dead had come to life, and that her lover had been restored to her. She only saw a life in danger, and the neces- sity for immediate action.

In an hour's time Arthur Holme was in bed, and had regained his senses. Lord Heather- stOne stood by his side, and questioned him kindly. They had parted in anger, but Holme's helpless conditidn would have ap- pealed to the hardest heart, and there was much real kindness hidden under the pompous and aristocratic manners of Lord Heather- stone.

Bit by bit, Holme told his story. At times he was a trifle incoherent, and he often had to stop. Lord Heatheittofie .did not press for details, but directly he had gathered the main facts he rang the bell. "Tell someone to go at'once to Gorehaven," he said, when a maid entered. "He must inform the police that Mr. Jordison, of the Red House, and his servants, must be arrested at once for the murder of the sailor. William Outen. In dase they may be too late,' send half a 'dozen of the men to the Red House at once to secure these 'scoundrels, and detain• them Until the police come. I will take all responsibility." The girl left the room, and Halme, tho- roughly exhausted, closed his eyes and slept. Lord Heatherstone went over to the window, and looked out across the marshes to where the Red House rose against the eastern sky. It was a clear, frosty morning, and he could see it plainly in the sunlight. He went intc his own bedroom and returned with a pair of ixiwerful field glasses. Then he opened the window and directed them on the ugly red brick building. Nothing stirred, but he could see smoke still rising from the stables, which appeared to have been burnt to the ground. :then suddenly a cloud of smoke and dust rose from the hilt, and several seconds afterwards there was a low boom, like the sound of a dis- tant gun. When the smoke cleared away, the Red tiouse was a low and shapeless mass upon the ground. He saw a black oblong thing move swiftly westwards along the road between the two creeks. He uttered a word which was neither parliamentary nor beconi- ing to a man of his position. In less than two minutes the moving object was hidden behind a Clump of trees on the liwn. Lord Heather- stone closed the window and went down to breakfast.
• By noon the six men had returned. They reported that they had not encountered a living soul on the road, and that the 104 House was a mere heap of ruins.

div.head: CHAPTER XXI. 111.14 AND CRY.
div.p: CHAPTER XXI. 111.14 AND CRY.

THERE was little doubt that three of the, murderers had escaped in the motor car, and that the fourth was dead. A body, charred and consumed beyond all recognition, had. been found by the police in the black ruins of the stables. There was no evidence to show whether it was the body of Jordison Or that of one of Ins three servants. No one knew of Susanson's death, and it was commonly sup- posed that three people had escaped. Holme, indeed, spoke of only having seen one of Jordison's servants, but it was well-known that there had been four men in the house, and it was not extraordinary that a person confined to the four square walls of a loose box should only have come in contact with two of thegn. The Red House hail tumbled down like a .house of .cards. Scarcely one brick was left sunding on another: It resenibled a vast rubbish heap, or a building that had gone through the hands of the house breakers. It wag no longer the semblance of a house, but a mere pile of brick, timber, and plaster. The police had no hope of finding any bodies in the ruins, for they knew that the house had not been inhabited for some time past, and that Jortlison and his Servants had made their home iii the stables and outhouses. But they,removed every brick till the surface was level with the garden. They did this as a matter of form, and did not pursue their in- vestigations into the cellars, which were entirely choked up with rubbish. They found no trace of anything, not even of a single piece of furniture. They came to the conclusion that it had all been fEmoved to the stables and that it had perished in the fire. There was an ' element of weakness in this theory, for it would have been hard to ppet a houseful of furniture. into the stables, but the theory had to serve in default of a better one. Both Lady Heathetstone and Arthur Holme were carefully questioned and cross-examined. The former withheld as tin math l anoiofor Jordison's real name and past history. The latter gave his evidence to the best of his ability, but slurred over the matter Of Arthur Sterious, as an unimportant detail, and some hallucination of Jordison's brain. Other minor witnesses contributed to the general stock of knowledge, and Lord lleatherstone stated what he had seen from the bedroom window. • The sum total of it all was that William Jordison and his servants were responsible for the murders of Lord Overcliffe and William Outen, and that three of them had escaped from the distuct on a very powerful motor- car. The latter had been seen on the old Roman Causev.-ay by two oyster fishermen, whose boat was lying up one of the creeks. And then all ti are of it had vanished as com- pletely as though it had been swallowed up in the ooze of the mashes. The Essex papers/ in commentin. on Ciz. case, said that the only ;Thsfarfory f7,PI vre of the whole affair was the fact Chat three such determined ruffians had escaped from the neighbourhood, and that the fourth was dead. To a" Hull Daily News " reporter, Mr. Staff said :—" I have suffered agonies from bleeding piles for three years. I could hardly walk about the town, let alone follow my busi- ness. When night came I dreaded going to bed, for I .knew I could not rest,and many is the time when I have bad to get up, so great and agonising was the pin. When day dawned even walking caused rue the greatest of pain, I cannot describe the agony, pain, and sweat- ing I suffered. Life became almost unbearAble. I tried everything I know of. I listened to the advice of my friends, but it was of no avail. I almost despared of ever being cured, and thought the complaint would be the end of me.

Fines and costs amounting in all to £4 4s. were imposed. WHOLESALE THIEVING AT WIDNES. . . . .

`bAt Widnes, on Monday, Samuel Showan (7.1), Mid- wood-street, was charged with stealing a cockerel value 58., the property of Alfred Fozzard ;a horse-clipping machine value 10a. 6d. the property of William Swin- ells ; and 32,1 b. of pork value 163.. the property of George Coupe, on divers dates during June. The cockerel apd machine were identilled, and Mr. Coupe in his evidence stated that he killed four pigs the day pre- vious and took three away. One was left in the slaughter-house and on going to his premises next morn- ing he found the hams roughly cut away. Prisoner tendered one for sale for 2s. 6d., and it was, because of the refusal to buy that the police were acquainted.— Prisoner was sent to gaol for three months.

div.head: WHERE EGGS COME FROM'.
div.p: WHERE EGGS COME FROM'.

Many people would probably be surprise] te know from what different and distant countries the eggs come which are used in English hons.nolds. Siberia exports encrmous quanties of both eggs and butter to Western Europe, and the name of Egypt is probably even more unfamiliar as an egg-producing country lot the English market. Yet during the last twelve months the export of eggs from Egypt very nearly amounted to the enor- mous total of 60,000,000, and of these only a seventh part were sent to other European countries than our own. The trade, moreover, is undergoing a period of depression at present, owing to the prevalence of chicken cheera on the Egyptian Loldings, and the unwillingness of the fellabeen to take ay preventive measures. On the other hand these Egyptian eggs now fetch more than double the price they did seven or eight years ago.—" Country Lite.'

Royalty at Cardiff Castle.—The Royal visit to Cardiff in convection with the South Wales University shows that no memories remain of the old coolness which .mice existed between Windsor Castle and Cardiff Castle. That arose in the time of the grandparents of thepresent Marquis of Bute in consequence of the death at Court of his great aunt, Lady Flora Hastings. That event occurred in the earlier years of Queen Victoria's reign, and such was the feeling in the family, that, when the Royal yacht appeared in Cardiff Bay, the blinds of the Castle were pulled down. Years softened these asperities, but the late Lord Bate never went much to Court. He,was the original of Lord Beaconsfield's" Lothair," and the fabulous wealth attributed to that personage was scarcely an exaggeration of the fortune he, and his father before him, amassed chiefly by the development of Cardiff. The 'motor honeymoon is perhaps the most• the shoulders and fastening with scallops down the fashionable at the moment, but any idea that strikes a note of originality is welcomed. Not long since, a I society bride and bridegroom started from the church doors for Central Africa, with the object of shooting I big game, while/more recently another happy pair of high degree went straight from the church to their yacht, for a cruise in the Mediterranean. Wedding Wreaths and Veils.—ln the arrangement of the wedding wreath and veil there ha been a vast improvement this season, and that " flattered " appear- ance, once so usual among brides, is now a rarity. In the first place. the heavy lace veil, is, happily, seldom in evidence, the lighter and more—infinitely more—becom- ing net or tulle specimens being preferred. Then, the majority of brides are following the example set by Royalty, and are wearing their yells thrown back. But the change most appreciated is the improved arrange- ment of the conventional orange blossom and myrtle. The flowers are carefully wired into the form of a high tiara, or Russian crown, from which the veil flows out the effect being charming and becoming in the extreme. Maliciously Spoiling Summer Frocks.—A particularly unpleasant form of summer madness is that which 'prompts certain wickedly-disposed persons to take a delight in maliciously spoiling the frocks of well- dressed women. For several seasons past, there have been complaints of this sort, and lately a few instances have been reported to the police by women who have had their summer dresses splashed with ink or other fluid, whilst out shopping or walking in the streets. Nor are such cases confined to London, as they are reported from different parts of the country, and it would almost seem as if these outrages had as much connection with the weather, as the epidemic of suicides which regularly breaks out in the summtr season. What the motive can be is difficult to guess, but it is hoped that when caught, an example will be made of the perpe- tratois of such malicious acts. front. About a Name. —There are signs of an agitation 'amongst the ever increasing community of typists, who object to be christened with the same name as is applied to the machine at which they work. When anyone speaks of a typewriter, the reference is commonly sup- nosed to be to the girl who operates it, and to be called " a thing," has always had a peculiar aggravation for the feminine mind. The profession is consequently beginning to simmer over this indignity, with a view to making a protest against it. " Typist " is certainly a better and more convenient word, and if the girls who get their living at this work prefer it, there seems no reason why they should not be so styled, instead of being called typewriters.

div.head: TH !BIWA COLLECTING.
div.p: TH !BIWA COLLECTING.

One of the queerest fads in the way of collecting articles is the collecting of the thimbles of women celebrities. One of the finest of these collections is that of a London society man, who has a cabinet full of dainty finger-shields; while Mrs. Vanderbilt rejoices in the possession of a veritable thimble of that excellent neecllewoman, Queen Elizabeth. This is the gem of her collection, although the latter contains a solid silver thimble worn by our Queen when a girl of fourteen, and a substantial "finger- shoe" of no less a person than the mother of our King.

div.head: LADY INSPECTORS.
div.p: LADY INSPECTORS.

The Home Office are sending two lady, in- %lectors to inquire into the alleged overcrowd- ing among the fisherpeople in the remotO island of 'Cast. Some of the cleverest and most charming of London's women workers are en- gaged as Government inspectors of factories and workshops. Exceptional qualities of mind and character are required for such an occupation, and great care is taken in the choice of candi- dates. It is not every well-educated girl who would care, for example, to take a cab late in the evening and drive to some dressmaking establishment, there to encounter the pro- prietress and inquire into a case of supposed excessive hours. The work done by the lady inspector is as valuable to the community as that of the lady doctor.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

PETITES TIMBALES OF MACARONI—BoiI ounces of Genoa macaroni in salted water till ic is tender; strain and cut it into small pieces; mix it in a stewpan with two tablespoonfuls of chopped cooked tongue, a chopped hard-boiled egg, a dessertspoonful of chopped parsley, and about a gill of white sauce; stir in a little cream. one whole egg, and two yolks; garnish some small darmle moulds with a ring of red tongue. in the centre of which put a round piece of truffle; fill the moulds with the macaroni; twist a greased paper over them, and steam them about half-an-hour. Serve the timbales with good white sauce poured round them. and garnish the centre with the remainder of the macaroni cut into small pieces, mixed with grated Parmesan, and heated in a little of this sauce. I believe that any woman or intelligence. .tact, and determination can convert a very, ordinary and commonplace man into that enviable per- sonage who is always spoken of in the papers as "one of our leading citizens."

div.head: MY FIRST GUINEA.
div.p: MY FIRST GUINEA.

In contributing to the interesting series of famous authors' confessions in " Pearson's Weekly" on" My First Guinea, and What I did with it,"Mr. C.J.Cutclifte Hvne writes : My first guinea in the writing line was earned from London tradesman who offered me that sum—and after some trouble was induced to pay 2,s.—for literary assistance in arranging the subject-matter to be printed on his wrapping paper." " He vended everything, from a sextant to a pearl necklace, and having no trick with the pen himself, he wanted all his qualifications set out appetisingly —by a university graduate if possible. He said I made a very good job of it, and I hoped that his recommendation would procure me further orders. But it didn't." " 1 had written about six long novels before this, together with ?cwt. of assorted articles, essays, plays, and poems, but none wanted them. The first cash return came as above." Among other well-known authors Mr. W. Clark Russell writes : " The first guinea I ever earned was included in a sum of ten pounds which I ' took up ' for wages after a -voyage to Australia in a sailing ship in which I had signed articles for one pound a month as fourth mate. I received the money in London, and, being in want of a tall hat, turned into Moses and Sons. New Oxford- street, whose windows werefilled with new hats, the tickets affixed. I bought a hat for half a guinea, and after riding with it on the top of an omnibus for about 'half an hour, the thing blew away into the road, and swam picked up covered with mud by the conductor, and I was mortified to find that the label—' Only look— ifis. '—was attached to it, and that I had ridden through the streets s, ith the price of my hat on me."

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.
J HOUSING REFORM.
A Lancashire and Cheshire Conference.

A Housing Conference, which was largely attended by representatives of Lancashire and Ctioshire trade unions, Socialist bodies, and co-operative societies, and organised by the Workmen's Nationll Housing Council. was held in the hall of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, Manchester, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. G. D. Kelley, secretary of the Manchester and Salford Trades Council was in the chair, and there were on the platform Mr. George Harwood, M.P., Mrs. Pankhurst, Mr. T. R. Marr, Mr. W. P. Bytes, and the secretary of the Council, Mr. F. Knee. Mr. Balfour wrote that his views on the housing problem had been publicly expressed at length on more than one occasion and in particular in the House of Commons on May 17, 1900, on the occasion of the second reading of the Housing of the Working Classes, Act (1805) Amendment Bill. Mr. Harcourt expressed the hope that the delegates would not lose sight of the vital importance of cheap building material in the solution of the housing problem.

The dia- airman said that the blame for the growth Of slum areas which had followed the great modern increase of population and the influx from the country into the towns lay with municipal councils. We were now reap- ing the fruit of their neglect and want of thought. The great thing was to impress on municipal bodies the necessity of taking a more active part in housing reform and of using the powers they already possessed towards that end.

The Secreaary (Mr. F. Knee) criticised Mr. Balfour's reference to a speech live years old, when the question i had been advanced so far n the meantime. He had heard that speech, in which Mr. Balfour had laid the blame for the slums on the rentpayers and not on the freeholders. It was, Mr. Knee said, as irrelevant to send them to it to-aay as it would be to refer them to Herodotus. He proposed a resolution of wide scope appeal- ing to the organised workers to grapple with the housing difficulty by inducing their trade unions and co-opera- tive societies to invest their funds in the provision of good houses for their me-nbers, and above all by bring- ing pressure to bear on the local authorities "so that the securing to every family the necessary amount of healthy house accommodation shall not be left to chance or private enterprise,but shall be accepted as the respon- sibility of the community." The resolution further urged that the action of the Central Government in relation to housing should "cease to be that of dila- tory supervision," but that its policy should he "to initiate and assist schemes for slum clearance and the provision of good houses, to improve and expedite the means for the acquisition of sites, to give the local authorities power to issue non-interest-bearing notes in payment for constructive works, and to make grants or issue loans free of interest from the Imperial Exchequer to the local authorities, or by a tax on site values to to provide cheap money for housing purposes." Mr. Carey (Wigan Trades Council) seconded the reso- lution. The housing problem in Wigan was, he said, very acute. He insisted on the necessity for a change in the composition of municipal bodies if there was to be a reform. At present those bodies were composed largely of property owners, who were naturally influ- enced by private interest. They needed intelligent working men in place of such representatives, and he deplored the fact that working men had so little trust in one another and were included rather to be jealous of comrades who showed public Spirit and ability than to support them. Mr. T. R. Marr traced the present evil of Manchester slums to the lack of a municipal sanitary policy in the early part of the nineteenth century. He too spoke strongly on the question of the reform of the constitu- tion of municipal bodies. He urged the delegates to work to get such an enlargement of municipal powers as would enable councils to control the development of building area, and to interfere when necessary iu build- ing schemes. He contrasted the position of munici— palities here and in Germany where municipal plans for the development of suburban areas were compulsory. Unfortunately, he said, slum areas were getting continu- ally overlooked. He gave an instance of a case in which some slum property he was acquainted with had been inspected and condemed twelve years ago, yet it still remained. He suggested that in every town hall there should be coloured plans of slum areas, drawn up by the medical officer of health, and that as improve- ments were made areas should be struck off. Then everyone would know what was being done. Mrs. Pankhurst spoke on tin! housing problem from the women's point of view. After all, she said, men were only lodgers, and it was the women who fully understood the terrible hardships of slum life. She urged that to such conferences in future representatives of the women's co-operative guilds should be invited. Reference, she said, had been made to the acquisition by municipalities of widerpowers to acquire land. What had struck her very forcibly was the criminal verly in which municipalities parted from th 2 laud they had She esked above all for an idealistic and not a petti- fogging treatment of the question. There was a wide possibility'of experiment.and she would like to see both the private house and the co-operative housekeeping system tried. A discussion arose on the clause in the resolution recommending trade unions and co-operative societies to invest their funds in the provision of good houses for their members, and Mr. J, R. Clynes (Oldham) moved that this should be omitted, which was agreed upon. Mr. Thomas (Liverpool) then objected to the clause recommending that the Government should give the local authorities power to issue non-interest-bearing notes for constructive works, substituting the words "by granting powers to municipal undertakings for the purpose of conducting re-housing or constructive works."

• Mr. Morrissey (Liverpool) seconded, but the amennd- ment was lost and the original resolution carried by large majorities. Mr. W. P. Byles moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and to the Co-operative Wholesale Society for the use of the hall, and in a short speech pointed out the relation of the housing question to the wider question of land ownership. Mr. George Harwood, M.P., seconded the vote. He had not, he said, come to speak but to learn; neverthe- less he would like to utter a brief word of warning. Whatever action was taken, he trusted that above all the working men of the country would preserve their dignity. He had a great suspicion of any scheme that would place them iria dependent position. He said, in conclusion, that ten years in the House of Commons had taught him the painful truth that its members confined themselves almost wholly to class lines of action. What was wanted in Parliament was a larger contingent of democratic men, who would do what was right and beneficial for humanity and not think solely of their class.

COMMERCIAL FAlLtrnEs.—According to the "Man- chester Guardian Society's Gazette, the number of commercial failures published in the United Kingdom during the quarter ending SAturday, June 24th, was 2,170. The number in the corresponding quarter of last year was 2,203, showing a decrease of 27, being a net increase in 1903, to date,ef 78.

div.head: WARRINGTON OPINION.
div.p: A WARRINGTON OPINION.

The opinion of a Warrington man has weight with ns,, especially when the opinion is based on actual experi- ence, as in this CASEI : Mr. John Dolan, who lives at 51, Foundry-street, War- rington, says :--" For over ten years I was simply a martyr to kidney complaint. My back was so dreadful that whenever -I stooped it was almost more than I could do to straighten myself again and the pains in. the region of my loins were indescribable. I became. so feeble that I was unable to walk, and had to take hold' of the furniture to get about the room. My appetite- was entirely upset, and I suffered dreadfully from dizzy attacks.

"At length, I became so bad that I was obliged to have medical advice. The doctors told me that I had strained my back. Having been employed for many years as a maltster, and daring that time often having had to work seven days in a week, I don't wonder at this—it was enough to try the constitution of a giant. got no better, however, until I began using Doan's Backache Kidney Pills, which were recommended to me by a neighbour. I had only been taking these pills a few days before the improvement in my health was very evident. The backaches were much less troublesome ; I was able to hold myself up, and walk well. Needless: to say, [continued using the medicine, and within short time I was in better health thin I had been for many years before. The credit for this entirely goes to Dean's Backache Kidney Pills, which I can recommend as the hest medicine I have ever COMA across in my life." Warrington P.S.A. Society. An open meeting of the above Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on San lay, when Mr E. Plinstnn occupied the chair. Mr. Smith sang with elect' The Man of Sorrows "and "Lead kindly light,"' being accompanied on the piano by Mr. T. Brough. The, Rev. J. Yonge gave an address on" Tne use and misuse of speech." One of the pleasures of life, he contended, was to be able to converse both in the outside world and in the family circle with the speech that rr,,s pure. If speech ViMS to be made pure we must be truthful,and this was possible with everybody. Then when we had overcome this evil we could depend upon respect from all. And there was the abuse of speech which was so common with the community to-day. Why should people in conversation use tllth sod absurd expressions, and taken God's name in vain? fie (the speaker) urged all present to use their inanenca in trying to pet a stop as far as lay in their pr, to this misuse of speech, And then, when we havegot purity of speech, we might look upon this Imd with pleasure, and all things would indeed be beautiful. (Applause.)

Wycliffe P.S.A. The usual weekly meeting was held on Snnclay. There was a poor attendance, accounted for by the heat. The hon. sepretary (Mr. B. Farrar), presided, and made special reference to three deaths that had taken place during the last week: Mr. James Efurkt of Parker- street, who had long been a member of this society; the wife of Mr. James Tanner also of Parker-street, after a long illness; also Mr. A. Dumbell, who had been a member for some time. The Chairman moved a vote of sympathy and condolence with the sorrowing friends or the departed. The vote was passed in the usual solemn manner. • Mr. W. H. Wharton, of :Manchester, was the speaker, and spoke to young men especially as "com- panions." Youth had great advantages for work, endur— ance, and activity. When opportunity was let slip then the wheels of time were hindered from more useful effort. If the great army of youth handed together,who could tell the good that could be done for God and, man? Mr. R. FI. Pearson gave two violin solos in a. pleasing manner; "Melody" and "Cavatina." Mr. W. H. Payton Mum. Bac., accompanied on the organ. Anniversary Services. I The Sunday school aaniver3ary sarvices in connection with the Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street, were- held on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. J. ' Humphries, of Leeds. In the morning a service was. held in the church, and in the afternoon a musical ser- vice was held in the Parr Hall. The chair was occupied by Dr. Ferguson, and the speaker was the Rev. J. F. Matthews. The Apollo Prize Male Choir, to the number of about 60 voices, rendered the following selections, under the conductor,hip of Mr. Ff. Berrey, and were greatly enjoyed :—" San of God," " Britons " (teat pieces), and "Crossing the Plain." The soloist was Miss L. Fairhnrst, who sweetly rendered "Come unto Me." At the evening service in the Parr Hall Mr. H. Berrey was the soloist, and he gave with reflect " Then shall the righteous shine." Special anthems and hymns. were rendered by children and choir under the conductor- ship of Mr. Nathan Cook. Sevaral members of the Apollo and Buckley-street choirs rendered. "The Heavens are telling " in a pleasing manner. The accom- panists were Miss Plinston arid Mr. A. B. Prow. The collections, which were in aid of the Sunday school,. realized about £2O.

Memorial Service. • A special service in memory of the late Mr. W. Gallop Wag held on Sunday morning in the Baptist Chapel, Golborne-street. The Pastor, the Rev. H. Dunnico took as his text, " And Enoch walked with • y God ; and he was not, for God took him." After general remarks on the • subject of walking with Ziod. Mr. Dunnico made special reference to the late Mr. Gallop, speaking of his connection with that church for forty-nine or fifty years, his name being one of the oldest inscribed on the church roll. He attended that church on the days of the Rev. Mr. Rowson, and after that minister's resignation worshipped in Butter- rmrket-street, then in Rylands-street, and then in 1877 returned once again to SalertvChapel, Golborne-street. He was broact in his views, bright and genial in dis- position, ever striving for peace, and generous, both in money and labour, in his support of the cause. Whilst he made no pretence of learning, be was a man of no. mean attainments. He was a great student of Patley, and had a vast and extensive knowledge-of the history,. growth and uses of _herbs. After referring to his last illness and the cheerful manner in which his sufferings were borne, the preacher said his death was a distinct. loss to the church, and urged the youtig people to greater zeal and to come forward and tale up the work as the elders were called to lay it down. Hymns suit- able to the occasion were sane, and at the close the organist, Mr. Trow, played the Dead March in"

A clause in the London County Council by-laws o; the Employment of Children Act requires that all boys and girls who carry on street trading, as newsboys, /tn., shall be compelled to call for their badge at a police station, the last place where a child should be seen.

My desk is laden with good wishes from boys and girls, and I don't think I can do better this week than reply to some of them. . . . . Walter Coxhead, although only ten, -sends me a very nice letter. One cold frosty morning something sad hap- ipened. Nothing perched on Elsie's pillow—no little Bully came to wake her up! When Mamma had looked everywhere around the room for him, she found him, at last, on the .‘mantel all cuddled up in a heap. She took him -very gently in her soft hand, but poor little Bully shivered when she touched him. She tried to make him stand up, but she found that none little leg was quite crooked. Poor Bully was lame from the cold

Little Elsie was so sorry! But Mamma thought she could help Bully, co she brought hot water .and bathed his poor leg. Then she put striae sort, white wool in his cage, and laid him down upon it, very tenderly. After a while Bully ,opened his beak, and gave .a. little "chirp, chirp I" When Elsie heard it, she sprang out of bed and said: "Oh I know he is hungry!" •

• Then ehe pattered about the room with her bare little feet, found the seed, and took some •in her fingers, and held it up to him. At first ;Bully would not take it; he scarcely opened his ,c.yee; but, after she had waited a little, he gave a sharp peck, and caught it from her hand. _Then Elsie gave him some more, and, after a Hull fell asleep. When •Elsie was •'dressed she went to look at him again. His ,eyes were open, so Mamma bathed his poor foot onee. more. . .

::con it was better, so that Bully could stand upon it quite well, and even hop about again; lmt Mamma was afraid to let him fly about the loom at night. And now Elsie must awake her- self in the morning, tpr Bully does not come to peck at her cheek
A childie once to its mother said, '6 Why is it we never see Uncle Ned?
"When come?"—and then a pause— " Does he belong to pa's side or yours? What is he like, has he curly hair?

• Or a great bald spot on the top of his head. ,Is he old or young, is he dark or fair? Or does he wear whiskers, our Uncle Ned 9," "Why is be Uncle?" said the wee little tot. "Are there three gold balls in front of his shop? Why doesn't he stay with us once or twice? •Why doesn't he send me something nice?" Said the mother with such a happy look, "If you guess all his puzzles he'll send you a
book. So • now do your best and try might and main, And don't bother me about Uncle again."
"Always nay as you go," said an old man to his nephew. "But uncle,' suppose I have nothing to pay with." "Then don't go," said '.-the uncle.

div.head: FLABBERGASTER. (Concluded.)
div.p: THE FLABBERGASTER. (Concluded.)

Then everyone' gave a key, and had their hands crossed by the Jester, after which he silently slipped out of the room, leaving King, Queen, Courtiers, and all gazing into their hands .to break, as they thought, the magic spell. Minutes flew by, and then hours, but never a sound of gong, until, in a rage, the King demanded that they search the rooms one by one for Jester and for mystic answer. Away they trooped, Ring and Queen, leading. Courtiers behind, and servants hindermost of all; room after room examined, but the search was in vain. Only one room remained, Ind that the Royal Treasury. The Lord Chief Money- spender was ordered to produce the key, but it was nowhere to be found. Then somebody suggested that it must have been the Treasury key given amongst others to the Jester. The King was blue with rage, and began talking of executions, meanwhile sending for the Court carpenters in order to burst open the door. This was done, and the door, once opened, everyone beheld the mystic answer illuminat- ing the wall. The answer ran— " Because the higher the flyer the fewer." __ .

Yes, the answer was there,- but the Imperial money wasn't, nor the Jester. The King broke out into a towering paseion, and everybody be- came frightened, but at last everybody had to admit that they had been had, the King, the Queen, the Courtiers, and even the drudges. The coffere were filled again in time, and every- body lived the usual happiness ever after, resolving, however, never to trust long-faced, melancholy people again. An execution takes place every time the word mouse is mentioned in the Imperial presence, land, as a warning, the captive mouse to this day remains stuffed in a special niche above the Royal Treasury doorway.

fUE A.ItT OF KISSING.

There is just one remark we . may make here, and that is the Siamese . do not kiss each other we au. ft is difficult to describe a. riatakese kiss, and not very easy to accomplish it very nicely—so I am told.—Yon place your nose gently against the lady's cheek and then give a mme or less vigorous sniff. It looks rather peculiar but it serves the purpose, and after all, all these things are purely !natters of custom. The marriage ceremonies last two whole days and it is not until the conclusion of the second day's festivities that the bridegroom gets speech of his bride. Early on the morning of the first day a great • feast is prepared and crowds of priests, friends, hnd hired musicians assemble to do honour to the event. Soon a sound of music is heard in the distance and the bridegroom's procesSion approaches. With him come troops of friends and more musicians. All are dressed in orange, purple, green, pink, and blue, making welly medley of colour, Which gains in bright- ness from the ever-present sunshine. The • bridegroom on his arrival goes to his new house and eats of the betel nut and other good things that have been- sent by his future wife. Pre- sently the marriage service begins, but a screen • separates the • hapny pair. They are sprinkled with rice, scented oil, and flowers, and then the screen is taken away. The priests pray and the couple kneel down to be bathed. The chief priest present, takes a bowl of water and pours the whole of its contenta aver, the head of the bridegroom after which be repeats the operation On the bride. He pronounces a blessing on them both and the ceremony is over. Feasting and dancing occupy the rest of the tday and at even ;- tide the visitors return to their homes. The young husband brings his band of musicians beneath his wife's window and there, with weird -strains from weird instruments, celebrates the lady's beauty and her virtues until the small ; hours of the morning.
A TWO DAYS WEDDING.

The second day begins like the first with twisting and song. But . towards evening an elderly and. respectable couple go to the new house and arrange everything for the lion e• coming of the newly married pair. The husband enters the house first, his arrival being preceded by a procession of his' friends bearing torches. Ilere he anxiously awaits his wife, and about nine o'clock she arrives with another troop'of -friends. All the people crowd around the pair and stay with them for a long time chatting and chewing betel nut and making themselves very much at home. But all things 4:oine to an end at last and one by one the visitors go home, leaving the young folks to themselves for the first time in their lives. Never, we may be sure were friends so gladly parted with as those who call their lust good-nights' as they step down the bamboo ladder and take themselves away into the night. A Siamegs often has. many, wives. It is only in the case of the first or head wife that all these formalities are observed. The other wives are merely goods and chattels,' and are bought with about as much ceremony and consideration as would attend the purchase of a house or a horse. A man may have as ninny wives as he can keep. Hence in • the prover classes it is customary for each man to have but one wife. It must not be thought that those wives that have been obtained by purchase are regarded as holding a. disgraceful position. Not, at all. Custom again declares that their position is an honourable and respectable one. But these subordinate wives do not hold as high a social position as 'the first pr head wife, and they fre- quently occupy a separate dwelling. They can also be sold'or given away. All the princes mid noblemen have large harems. The late king had eighly-four children, who were the offspring of thirty-five smothers. The present king is the father of an equally large family:

div.p: (ALL RIORTS rtEBFIVED.I HOW THEY GO A-WOOING
IN SIAM,
E. YOTING. (Author of" The Zngdout Of The Yellow liGbe,"

Perhaps there is 130 subjectMch interests sO many people all the world over as that of love, courtship and marriage. In every clime the men make lore, the women return the cdra• plimeut, and marriage follows. Or perhaps it would be truer to say, that in every clime, men seek a wife or wives, and that either by love or purchase they generally attain their end..

In all such itifitirs, as managed -in the far off land I write about, courtship, is a very import- ant business. but one in which the lady counts for very, little. As she is generally married be. tween the ages of •fourteen and sixteen it is evident that she is not old enough, perhars, to be consultel about her future welfare. •Her would-be husband is not oftener more than twenty or twenty one. Let me hasten to add at once that there are pi) old maids in ,Siam, and that therefore every girl gets married to somebody sooner or later.
‘SIAM!:SE ELOrEMENT:

It occasionally happens that a Siamese youth sees a 6iamere maid who awakens in him the warmest affections. Now they can elope it' they like. In such a .case they run 'away to- gether, stay away z few days, and then return and beg. forgivenessr They • visit no Registrar, and no Parson ; but they are every bit as much married bw. their own act as if they had gone through all the ceremonies I am about to describe. Of course such a proceeding as the above is highly irregular, and is not usually resorted to in the best vciety. In the ordinary and conventional method of proceeding the- young lover is particularly rtreltil to say nothino. of MI intontimis to the lady of his choice. Should he ,do so he would probably be suspected of improper intentions, and the young lady's fat-her or brothers would promptly undertake the persona) chastiseinent of the love-sick sWilb. If he desires to secure the lady's affections as well as her hand he cm; purchase from some quack an effective love potion. This he can scheme that the young lady shall drink,. and after that she would know no peace until her lot had been united with .his.

The first formal proceeding to be taken is for the young man to tell his father, whom he wishes to marry. A family 'council ensues and if the young mauls fancy is approved by his relatives they choose a discreet and elderly lady who is acquainted with both /families. This ambosadress makes a formal call upon the lady's parents, sips her tea, with becoming delibera- tion, and when a favourable monent occurs generally discloses the purpose of her visit. Nothing decisive ever immediately follows the lisclosure, but the mother of the girt will con- vey some. idea as to whether the proposed ;iv ungement is distasteful or not. If - she indicates that tt• formal proposal might be favourably considered the young man's friends choose a kind of small committee from amongst themselves. They hold a •little tea party at which they disc:Liss the contemplated marriage in all its bearings • and finally decide whether it in the be interests of their yowl,- friend that he should proceed further with the mutter.
A voRmAL rwirosAL.

Let us suppose that they all vote for a wedd- ing. They afterwards go in a body to the home of Phyllis and wait upon her parents. They are received with every attention, mid the . Siamese equivalent for five o'clock tea " is lispensed. When sufficient food has disappeared the spokesman of the Mission, in very formal tones, says something like the following ".The parents of having ascertained that this is a propitious day, have commissioned us to come and confer with you concerning, their son, who at presAt has no wife. llis parents have asked him if he had anyone in his mind that he would like to take for his wife, mid to whom he could trust his life in sickness, and his obsequies after death. The young man replied that the only person he had in his mind was your daughter of the name of ------Therefore at the request of the parents of ibis young man we are here to visit you, .the highly respected parents of this young lady, that we may confer with you in reference to this matter. What do the parents say P" . . _

Irhe parents, with similar stilted, mid formal language give answer after this fashion " Our daughter stands high in our affections and the young man is also much ,beloved by his parents. We have an ancient proverb which says Move slowly, and you will gain your object ; a pro- longed effort is usually • attended with favour- able results.' We will consult with our relatives on the right hand mid on the left hand and take their counsel and opinion upon the matter. Please call again."
A DEI:IDERATE CONSIDERATION.

This is the end of the first conference. After I a suitable pellod of waiting, the iiommittee in' sharge of dip male lover's interest pays a second visit to the girl's parents. We will •suppose ' that the course of true love has so fn. run ' :•ittioothly, that the match is entertained favour- ably on both sides, hi this case the visitors ire greeted as follows We have consulted our relations and they are unanimously -of the opinion that if the young man loves our daughter, and if he can place implicit confidenCe in her as a proper person to tend him in sickness, and direct` his funeral ceremonies after death, then we will no longer place any barrier to the attain- nient of his wishes. But how is it with regard to the '\ ages and the birthdays of the parties F Are they such as are suitable to each other P 9 This last question. has no reference to the ages (*the •young people, because there is never -any very great discrepancy .in age. It has refer- ence to a peculiar i4amese custom. Accord- ing to the tiiamese every year is under the in- fluence of .some animal. They have a cycle of twelve years ruled over -in succession by the Rat, Cow, Tiger, Rabbit, Major Dragon, Minor Dragon. Horse; Goat, Monkey, Cock, Dog, and Hog. Now it is deemed very undesirable that persons should marry it born in certain years. A girl who was born. in \ the year of the Rat, might Conceivably. have a very, .unhappy time with a husband who was born in the year of the Dr, though those of the Goat and tAie•Rabbit might live very peaceably together. This ,very important question is settled by an astrologer, who for a sufficiently large donation will in- variably declare that the two parties may safe- ly be joined in matrimony. Fortified with the decree of the astrologer. the committee seek another and final meeting for the consideration of other details,

div.head: TILE' QUESTION OF SETTLEMENTS.
div.p: TILE' QUESTION OF SETTLEMENTS.

The girl's parents remark " Since birthdays need cause no further delay What shall be said about the money to be provided for' the young couple to commence business on, aud the money for building a house. for their habitation ?" Every intending bridegroom 'mist either possess a house, or signify Ins willingness to erect one previous to his marriage. If a house has to be built, it is, when possible, erected near to the home of the girl's parents. It thus happens that if a man has many daughters and Plenty of laud, he may ultimately be surrounded hy • small colony of descendants and the •e mother-in-law is able to keep a watch- • upon the dolngs of each and all of hex 015- in- law;. _

At this final conference they 'settle the amount' of money which. each, of the contracting parties is to provide, and they also arrange how it is to be spent. They plan the future abode of the wedded pair, and decide on the number of rooms and the amount of furniture they are to contain. They discuss the wedding feast and they arrange bow many dishes shall be pro- vided by the bridegroom, and his friends. When he last detail has been finally accepted by both mrties, the young lady is informed that she, is o be married. -

It madit reasonably bare been supposed that the engaged. couple would oe permitted to confer with one another, to talk those bliss- ful nothings that take so long to say, and which bear incessant repetition, to discuss their future life, and to quarrel and make up again, as is the wont of then%European brothers and sisters. But no, not a word do the betrothed even whisper to each other. If the enamoured swain would send his sweetlieart a message or a &ft he must send it through her parents. Until the marriage ceremony IF4 completed the pair are supposed never to meet, and never to see each other. Should the lovers be over ardent, and transgress these stringent regula- tions, the whole business Would collapse.

div.head: DIVORCE.
div.p: DIVORCE.

Getting divorced is easier than getting married. Divorce is procured merely by mutual consent. The wife then returns to her parents taknig with her all the property she possessed at the time of her marriage, and also all that she may have since acquired by gift. purchase, or trade. She takes also • the first, third, and fifth of her children.

Siamese women are good tempered, gentle and winning in their manners, end make .ex- eellent • wives aid mothers. They would pOssibly make very charming sweethearts else, did custom permit them to Adopt sueli a ride. As it is they ' never have the supreme pleasure of eiternately tormenting' end h.imdliiig the one to whole they will one day entreat their happi- ness mid their lives.

THE UNMARKED TOMB IN HOOTON ROBERTS
CHURCH.

The work was put into the hands of a skilled mason, and one morning he came to tell me that two bodies, Very much decomposed—in fact, all dust except a few bones—had been found just under the flags. 13 jog north and south, not east and west; and now another coffin had appeared ins similar position. I went to the church, and found that immediately in front of the communion table a burial had taken place; as I stood in the trench, I conld trace the outline of a coffin in the dry soil, its shape being that of a casket with sloping lid and sides. A fragment of the wood of the coffin showed that it had originally been studded with brass nails, and probably covered with cloth. The end of the coffin had fallen out, and a skull could be seen through the dust. When touched with the hand the skull fell into the trench, leaving the vertebra exposed. The mason put down his hand to gather them up -and place them on the communion step. I was examining the skull at the moment, when the mason exclaimed, 'Why, one of these vertebra has been cut clean in half!" At that time any thought of finding Lord Strafford's body had never crossed my mind,although I knew Lady Strafford was buried somewhere in the church; even when I saw the cut vertebra I did not at once realise the troth. This only dawned upon me afterwards when I had examined the bona.; of the other bodies. Before reach- ing the body in front of the communion table, the workmen had found two others in line with it on the South side. Both were very much decayed ; but one skull was perfect, and was undeniably that of an old woman, other bones were those of a young person. Their appearances corresponded with the ages of Lady Strafford and her daughter, Lady Margaret, who died, as have said, a girl of sixteen.—" From " Lord Strafford's Burial Place" in the' Cornhill Magazine" for July.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JULY lit 1905.
Th o Statutory THE STORES SCANDAL Commission, as it DEBATE. is now constituted,

gives satisfaction to the general public, who will have full confluence in ne impartiality of the tribunal. If Mr. BALFOUR had appointed it immediately after the Butler Report, instead of fencing and juggling as he did, he would not have lost so much credit with the moderate men of his Own party. The immoderate men, whose organ is "The Daily Telegraph," assure him that he has done no wrong, and that his opponents are bitterly disappointed because the character of the Commission is so high and the terms of reference so comprehensive. But it is not the character of the Commission that is in question. It is the question of the Government. Mr. BRoDRICK tried to prove that when he was at the War Office he did everything that could be reasonably expected. He was even prepared to give evidence before the Butler Committee, and he could not understand why he was not called as a witness. As there was not the smallest doubt that Mr. BRoDRICK would have been called if he had intimated any indisposi- tion to assist the inquiry, why did he not make that intimation F It was a very curious omission on his part.He quoted Lord KITCHENER'S opinion about the value of the stores, but the Government were careful not to ask for a report from Lord KITC HENER on the whole transaction. ARNoLD•FoRsTBR was asked whether Lord KITCHENER'S evidence as to the system of accounts which he set up at Pretoria had been mis- laid, and AnNorm-FonsrEit said it had not. The allegation is that the system was ignored after Lord KITCHENER had left South Africa. I

Surely his testimony on this point is of some importance, and we trust that the Commission will call for it. Mr. BRODRICK asserts that the War Office in his time exercised due vigilance and supervision. He certainly did ask for a monthly return of all the sales and purchases of stores ; but be did not get that return, and Mr. BRODRICK failed to explain to the House why the War Office acquiesced in the flat disobedience of its orders. That there was culpable waste, if nothing worse, Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTER admitted. Mr. BILODRICK said he had been compelled to censure certain officers for incompetence. The Secretary for War spoke of men who had been called upon to perform duties for which they were unfitted. But why was the discovery of their unfitness made so late? What was the War Office about between Septem- ber, 1903, when, as Sir ROBERT REID pointed out, there were the gravest misgivings, to January of the present year, when Mr. ARNOLD-FORSTE found it necessary to oppoiut the Butler Com- mittee? Although the Government admitted that there was a serious waste, it is evident that for some time they regarded the disposal of stores as the natural course of business. A correspon- dent of the " Times," who says he has read the evidence before the Butler Committee, asserts that there waa "no avoidable loss." He takes it as a natural order of things that Government stores should be sold for next to nothing to contractors and bought back again at a profit to these contractors estimated at £2,000 on a single days transaction. " The Times " tells us its correspondent is a person of authority. P,rhaps it is Mr. BRODRICK himself who says Sir WILLIAM BUTLER'S Report is melo- dramatic. What must lat: its character, ie the eyes of any man who thinks there has been much ado about nothing, and that the nation on the whole has no cause for complaint. The late Secre- tary for War and his successor both admit that some officials had to be censured for their failure in duties for which they were responsible, but the incapacity was nearer home, as the debates made abundantly clear.

Our Conservative contemporary, the Warring- ton and District Licensed Victuallers Wine and Beer Trade Association, and various other people have jumped to the conclusion that Mr. A. H. Crosfield was so incautious last week as to state that there were a number of shady drinking-shops in Warring:on. We need hardly say here that Mr. Crosfield said nothing of the kind, for his friends entirely disbelieve the story. In fact not even the " Observer " reports Mr. Crosfield as making such an assertion, though it is read into his remarks very ingeniously. Our contemporary and other hasty people stand self-condemned of a lamen- table indiscretion equal to that with which they would charge Mr. Crosfield. The " Observer" quotes Mr. Crosfield as follows: " We should do what we can to lessen the temptation to excessive drinking by clearing out a lot of shady drinking shops which are not wanted in Warrington. We will try to bring this about."

Now, while this is not Mr. Crosfield's reference verbatinz et literatim it is sufficiently accurate in itself to show than the speaker is innocent of the " serious allegation" attributed to him. We ask our reauers, and our 2ontemporary also, does Mr. Crosfield say there are sbady-drinking shops in Warrington, even in the above version of his speech ? Toe answer is plainly, and mith little cogitation required,—No !

None of the three Warrington papers reported Mr. Crosfield in the first person singular, which is the only way of rendering a man's remarks exactly as he utters them. Our owe.: reporter, however, took a full note of the speech in the form in which it was uttered, and the disputed passage in his notes reads as follows: " Education, like temperance, will follow in the wake of land reform, though I would say in the meantime, what we can do to lessen the temptations towards excessive drinking by clear- ing out a lot of shady drinking shops, which are not wanted in Warrington, we will try to bring about." Mr. Crosfield was speaking generally, and he only localised his remarks by tacking on the harm- less allusion to such drinking-shops not being wanted in Warrington. The sentence is rather , involved, but we think it will be perfectly clear to any unbiased and reasonable person that the idea of there actually being shady drinking-shops in War- rington never crossed the speaker's mind. The whole tenour of tha speech at this point was in the direction of framing temperance legislation—a positive proof of its generality, fur such legislation will not be called into being specially on War• rington's behalf. Shady drinking-shops are a ' national menace and Mr. Crosfield was quite within his rights in drawing attention to them in the way he did. We are convinced that he neither made nor intended to make any reflection on War- rington' and the closest scrutiny of his remarks acquits him of having done so.

Although women have no direct voice in national affairs, they can undeniably play a useful part in political work, and Liberalism in Warrington owes much to the active support which it receives from the Women's Liberal Association. The lighter side of politics is not over-looked by the members, and their annual picnic on Monday was a splendid success. It was a huge party which invaded the famous gardens at Belle Vile, and once more the men—although there was a very fair sprinkling—were in a hopeless minority. Belle Vue abounds in pleasing attractions, and the hours slipped by all too quickly. On such occa- sions speech.enaking takes a minor place in the programme of events, but after tea there were one or two interesting speeches which were just in the right vein. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who had a most flattering reception, Miss Potts (National Reform Union) and Mr. Howes showed how deeply the great questions of the day concern the women, and emphasised that it was to their interest, as chancellors of the home exchequer, to help to maintain Free Trade and cheap prices.

"What does England propose to do ?" is the pertinent question asked by the Rev. F. Lewis Donaldson, M.A., " chaplain " to the Leicester unemployed who recently marched to London. Mr. Donaldson has issued a brief but interesting account of the pilgrimage, and the condition and behaviour of the men who took part in it. He says : " Our journey to London must not be taken too literally; our march was a sacramental one, symbolising the cry ot the workless and poor throughout Eugland." These men were not loafers, but "ordinary working class citizens of Leicester, poverty-stricken by unemployment," and their chaplain comments on the folly and wickedness of lumping all the unemployed together and thinking of them as wastrels. At least three-fourths are, he says, honourable citizens, and he adds, "England must face this fact in determining her policy and her laws."

the omission of it has had sad effects which could be pointed to in innumerable instances. Teachers, as a rule, are not given to undue use of the rod, and it is essential that every one of them who is capable of taking a class should be empowered to compel discipline in the usual way. What a generation of namby-pambies we should be respon- ' Bible for if we neglected to make clear in early life 1 the fact that wrong-doing is followed by unerring and often swift retribution.

div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

To-morrow (Friday) is the children's day of days. SV alliing Day is an institution to which they all look forward with keen anticipation. We hope that the fine weather will continue and that the day will be spent happily and free from accidents. * * *

To-day (Thursday) the representation of Ease Finsbury will be decided. Mr. J. Allen Baker, L.C.C., who is contesting the seat in the Liberal interest, is a. gentleman in the truest sense of the word. He is an active helper in all good work and we wish him success: * *

Addressing a meeting at Preston the other evening, Mr. J. T. Macpherson, the Labour candidate for tha borough, stated that the Union Jack was the emblem of freedom, yet we took it out to South Africa to do away with white labour and introduce Chinese slaves. *s*

The third test match between England and Australia commences at Leeds on Monday next. There are five Yorkshiremen in the thirteen English players from winch the team will he selected, and two La.ucastrians, and yet Lancashire is the champion and only un- defeated county for two seasons.Brearley has,or should have a prior claim to Warren.

* * * Last week we indulged in a day trip to Blackpool per London and North Western Railway from Bank Quay. The early morning train left at 8.35 with some promptitude but at ten o'clock we had got no further than Wigan. One hour and a half for a dozen miles on a day excursion ! This is like the London and North Western's want of attention to detail. Ap- parently it was just an accident that there was any through connection at all before mid-day, * * *

About 960 women Liberals invaded Belle Vue on Monday under the auspices of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association. The way they were accommodated there should have been a lesson to the Railway Company, but it was not. Oh returning, at nearly midnight, the officials at Arpley Station col- lected tickets singly at the narrow exit door, with the result that the excursionists were put to a lot of delay and inconvenience. * * *

Mr. Will Crooks, M.P., raised a great laugh in the _House of Commons on Tuesday last, lie asked the Premier whether the Unemployed Bill would take precedence of the redistribution resolutions. Mr. Balfour in reply stated that "They are not in pari motet., a." Mr. Crooks could not understand the Latin and asked for it to be translated into English. Mr. Balfour gave what he called a loose translation which however did not satisfy- Mr. Crooks who remarked amid loud laughter, that it was certainly " very loose but not lucid."

There is many a true word spoken in jest. At the Education Committee meeting on Monday, Mr. Henry Roberts pointed out that Alderman Bennett, Mr. A. J. Jolley, and himself were shareholders in a company whose tender was before them" an toerlore Ozer could not vote ol ibis question." The contract may have been small, but the principle was fought for and recognized a year ago and is involved just the same. We are glad to see these evidences of an awakening; public conscience even if they are the basis of o little joke. . .

* * * Though 440 men comprised the Leicester unem- ployed pilgrimage to London, they did not add one to the number of unemployed in the Metiopolis. less than 421 returned, 10 found work en route, ana the rest were from time to time invalided home. Or" of the 440 it was found that 160 had been soldiers in the army, a percentage which points to the melancholy fact that England concerns herself but little with the men who have fought and suffered for her, once they have fallen from the ranks. * * We have been taken to task for our remarks last week on the admission of pupil teachers to the baths at a reduced charge. A well-known wielder of the rod and chalk in a large elementary school wants to know why the pupil-teachers should not have some conces- sion seeing that Corporation officials get a free ticket. Two blacks do not make a white—even in the baths. We should say that Corporation officials have less right to a cheap bathe than even the pupil teachers- Unless there is free-bathing for all, the only concessioa should be on behalf of the school children and the more accommodation they have and the better.

* * Quite a sensation has been caused this week by the inquest on two young children, and the verdict, of the jury that " the children died from exhaustion after fever and diarrhcea, set up by taking liquozone." This is a serious reflection on a largely-advertised patent medicine, and some further information relative to the properties of the preparation is called for in the interests of the public. it will probably have been noted that tho medical evidence at the inquest wag contradictory, so that the iinding of the jury is not conclusive proof that liquozone is dangerous. For the present it would be well for the people who have found the medicine efficacious to be cautious in its use.

* * Last week we called attention to the firm stand which Mr. Coroner Brighouse in taking on the subject of the state of minds of suicides. On Mbnday Mr. Gibson, the Manchester City Coroner, gave expression to similar views. He remarked that though many jurieti were prone to the belief that the mere commission to suicide was evidence of insanity, he had come to the conclusion, after careful consideration, that such wa9 not the case. It was a stigma, too, which ought r!ot to be cast on the remaining members of a family' unless there was evidence of it. In the case under review at the time there was no evidence of melan- cholia or depression and the jury returned a verdict of suicide. * * *

! " Beautiful Warrington "is a long way from being an accomplished fact but a Society with this pre- possessing title has been successfully launched. Some- day, perhaps, thanks to: the initiative energy of Mrs. Iliggs,of Oldham and Warrington enthusiasts who have co-operated with her Warrington may be beautiful as manufacturing towns go. The idea is an excellent ono and may yet render Mrs. Higgs famous. In eye*. community there is an inherent love of the beautiful which only wants arousing to be productive of the greatest good. The training of the towns to wash their faces, comb their hair, and put flowers in their buttonholes is a practical scheme which should eventu- ally change or abolish the oppressing sameness and. sordid griminess characteristic of our manufacturing centres. * * *

Mr. Lloyd George had a magnificent reception on Tuesday evening when he spoke in East Finsbury on behalf of Mr. Allen Baker's candidature.
