Shortly after noon an Wednesday a severe 'thunder- torni broke over Warrington. There were heavy peals of thunder, preceded by flashes of lightning, and rain came down in torrents. —ln the Mirshhouse•lane

district two houses , were struck 'by lightning. The Louse Mr. Joseph Langley, of 40, Gorssy-lane, was found to be badly damaged, all of the chimney stacks And pots were destroyed, and a quantity of slates torn off the roof. Inside the house tho fireplace in the front room was torn from its fastening and thrown across the room, the ornaments and furniture being <laman.'sed and broken. Mrs. Langley was cleaning the window in the room at the time, and had a narrow Ilscape. Only a few minutes previously her little baby ilad been playing against the fireplace, and she had sent her into another room. The house next door was also seriously damaged, the lightning tearing a large hole about a yard square in the roof and calling of the front bedroom. "The Little Warhorse, as the rabbit is called, knew 1-!actically all the dogs in town. First, there was a very, large brown dog that had partied him many times, - 'jog that he always got rid of by slipping through a %Mall hole in a board fence. Second, there was a small, Zetiye dog, that could follow through that hole, and him 0 baffled by leaping a twenty-foot irrigation ditch that "ald steep sides and a swift current. The dog could not rake this leap. It was sure medicine for him, and the still call that place " Jacky's Jump.' But there '4B a greyhound that could leap better than the jack, ;and When he could not follow through a fence, he could 4f,11111P over it. He tried the Warhorse's mettle more than -11ce and the sack only saved himself by his quick "glng„ tal they got to an Osage hedge, and here the hound had to give it np. Besides this there was in a rabble of big and little dogs that were troubler -"le, but easily left behind in the open. “ lts, tea country there wts a dog at each farmhouse, Only one that the Warhorse really feared—that was big, fierce ball-greyhound, a creature so swift and tertinacioua that he had several times forced the War- ...„°.riae to his final shifts to escape. In him the Warhorse lit have found his fate bat for a curious adventure a happy ending for the jack."—For the test of this 114aaresting animal -story by Ernest Thompson Seton fr the June "Windsor Magazine," the remarkable open- g number of a new half-yearly volume, containing the 'rat of a racy new series of yarns by Robert Barr. and Zl)roPlete stories by Jnstus Miles Forman, Halliwell '3l,tcliffe, and other favourite novelists, in addition to large instalment of Rider Haggard's wonderful narra- .trae of "flhe Return of 'She." "Railway Employment" :,,r;as the latest subdivision of the valuable survey of d matters, and Another natural history subject is Lthett call y dealt with by Charles G. D. Roberts. §cheol-Boy "waxes qnaintly eloquent " Concern- g cket " and the fine-art feature of the number is sixieen-page section of Fred Morgan's famous laactures of child-life and rustic scenes. Altogether it a% superb summer number.

div.head: WALKING DAY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.
ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE PROCESSIONS.

On the eve (Thursday) of the great children's festival one thought is uppermost in in the minds of yo4ng and old alike— Will it be fine ?" The brilliant summer weather of the past fortnight has buoyed the townspeople with the highest hopes, and present indications are that Dame Fortnne will not cease to smile on us at the last moment. The thunder- storm of yesterday has cleared the atmosphere some- 'what, and to-day there is once more bright sunshine. The youngsters are revelling in gleeful anticipations of the events of the day of days so far as Warrington is concerned. They, at any rate, are gifted with, a cheery optimism, and visions of new finery, pretty processions, and frolics in the fields, are their constant theine. Walking Day is the embodiment ,of true delights to Warrington children, and who would grudge them this annual treat? He indeed would have more boldness than discretion win would venture to suggest that Warrington could do very well without its Walking Day. Te-m n-row the dulness of our streets will be pleasantly relieved by picturesque pagdants, and the whole town will give itself over to enjoyment. At an early hour children will be seen making their way to the Sunday schools—the meeting places of happy and expectant throngs. Parents will have spared no effort in order to provide some new attire in which the little ones shall figure proudly. In many instances, it is true, the effort involves sacrifice, but it is cheerfully borne, ,and, however straitened the resources, there aki few h ones in which Walking Day &re not sea some new article .of summer finery. With bands playing and banners flying a start will be made for the Town Hall —the place of assembly for the Chnrch of Englanld and Nonconformist schools partici- pating in the main pracession. On the lawn the scene will be an animated one. The task of marshalling the youthful processionists will be undertaken by Coma- cillor J. G.Craik and Mr. Eric Fairclough.At ten o'cleck the scholars will begin to file through the central gate in the folloving order (n Blue Coat School and Band. "(2) Padgate Industrial School and Band. (3) Parish Church and St. Helen's Church, Holinfare, and Crostield's Band. St. George's Mission and Lvmm' Band. 5) St. Crement's Mission and Church Lads' Brigade Bugle Band. (16) Legh-street and Sharpe-street (P.M.) and Legh- street Band. (17) Salvacion Army and Band, (18) Ragged School and Drum and Fife Band. So far as can be gathered from the particulars sap- tilled by the school officials, the procession will not present many new features. It will be imposing mainly as a demonstration of strength, but will be sure to interest the thOusands of spectators—most of them parents and friends of the children—who will line the route. Eacts school will be headed hy a large banner, and the children will carry innumerable small flags. The teachers of St. Peter's school have again displayed acceptable origin- ality, and a number of children in pretty Swiss costumes war add variety to that school's procession. As usual thare will be gaily decorated lorries, drawn by smartly- caparisoned horses, and laden with smiling youngsters. The procession will traverse the usual route—that is, from the Park Gates along Parker-street, Wilson-Patton- at., and Bridge-st., to the respective schools. The Mayor has issued the usual order prohibiting vehicular traffie during the time of the procession, and the event should ' pass off without a hitch. At the Parish Church and several other churches short services will be held on the conclusion of the march round the town, and in the afternoon the children will adjourn to pleasant fields to disport themselves to their hearts' content. As in previous years most of the Nonconformist schools will content themselves with a processioa along a short route of their own, their intention being to give the children a complete day's enjoyment an the country. For instance, Wycliffe scholars will journey to Dunham Hill; Golborne-street Baptists to Lyinna ; Bold-street We.sleyans to Grappen- ' hall; Workingmen's. Mission and Sankey Bridges Westeyaris to Burtonwoed;•Cairo-street unitarians to Walton Old Hall; and Friars' Green and Brick-street Independent Methodists to Padgate.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION.
div.p: THE ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION.
Some of the Soecial Features.

For picturesquepess and brilliance of display the palm is always willingly* conceded to tne Boman Catholics who make especial effort on this annual occa- sion. Their procession is the result of much painstaking preparationond true artistic taste is brought to bear in the arrangement of the many features which please the eye of the spectator. It is fully expected that to-morrow's procession will enhance the reputation which.the schools enjoy in this respect,—in fact the display promises to excel anything previously attempted As uaual the pageant will take place shortly after the the Church of England and Nonconformist schools have traversed their complete route, which means that the children will leave their respective schools at about eleven o'clock. Bridge street is the only thoroughfare in which the spectacle can be witnessed quite in its entirety, for having met at Bridge foot the various schools leave the route at points convenient for reaching their respective churches. Banners of fine texture and workmanship are among the most striking features of the Roman Catholic pageant. To-morrow the works of art which have so often delighted the people of Warrington will once more be borne aloft.. Some will be embleniatio of the Sacraments of the Church, while others will depict the Blessed Virgin and the Saints. The superb grouping of the children and uniformity of costumes will render the display the more imposing. St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street will make a splendid effort and the chief banner will bear a reproduction of Marino's " Immaculate Concep- tion." The most beautiful feature of the procession will be a new statue of the Madonna and Child in pure white. The base will be covered with lovely flowers, and from it will be suspended streamers which will he carried by three hundred girls tastefully attired in white and other delicate colours. St. Alban's and St. Benedict's schools will as usual present a charming picture, and there will be magnificent floral devices and tastefully decorated sacred statues. The infants of St. Benedict's will carry gilt crosses decked with choice flowers. Many of the children accompanying St. Mary's, Latchford, will wear veils and wreaths, and a beautiful statue of the Sacred geart I will he borne by some of the scholars of the Church of the Sacred Heart. The general effect of the pageant will be most pleasing and, if we might give a word of advice to the spectators, it would be that. they should keep to the footpaths and allow the processionists temple room, as the effect may be seriously marred by unnecessary crowding towards the centre of the road.

The afternoon will be spent in a field at GrappenhAll Heyes, where games, sports, &c., will be indulged in.

SALVATION AIM' :—Established 1882. Number of scholars on books, 33 boys; 87 girls; average attend- ance, 303 weekly; number of tetchers, 14; Adjutant A. Searles, commanding officer; J. Ferguson, S.A. ; L. Dickinson, treasurer. Assembling at the Barracks, the scholars will march from Academy-street to the Town Hall and from there to the ptrk by the ordintry route. Dinner and tea. will be provided for 1,500 poor children. Games will be indulged in and there will be scrambling for sweets, and races .t.c. The workers are doing their utmost to mike the afternoon and evening enjoyable and given fine weather there is little doubt that their effort will be successful. The band will be in attendance.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
INCREASES OF SALARY DISCUSSED. The Accommodation Question.

A meeting of this Board was held nt the Workhonse on Wednesday, Mr. J. Billings presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Miss Broadbent, Rev. Dr. MeNer, Dr. Murray, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. W.Hickman, A. 7:Jolly, R. Forshaw, S. Davies, T. H. Ashcroft, T. Ritchie, W. Flanagan,'G..Mather, W. Houghton, A. Brooks, G. Thompson, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Pad gate schools).

div.head: INCREASES OF SALARY.
div.p: INCREASES OF SALARY.

Mr. MATHER moved the salaries of the Superintendent and Matron be respectively increased as from June 25th, by £5 per annum, and the salary of Miss Dyke (girls' industrial trainer) by £2 10s. per annum. Ho said that six months ago most of the officers of the institution applied for an increase of salary because the work had increased and tho number of children in the homes wilS a great deal larger than it was two years. It was unani- mously resolved to defer the question for oix months and at the adjourned meeting the present recommenda- tions were unanimously agreed to. Mrs. CLAY Leconded and Mr. BENT supported. . .

Mr.-THOMPSON moved that the quesiiroi be referred back to the Committee. They ought to have full,: particulars as to why the salaries should be increased/ for they had neard from Mr. Mather that it was very likely that it the increases were granted other appli- cations would follow. He thought there were other officials in the Union quite as deserving of an increase as the master and matron at PaJgate. He would like the committee to go thoroughly into the matter, as increases were serious things in these times. He was surprised at Mr. Mather bringing the matter forward after having recently stated that if they could keep the expenditure down the least bit it would be an ad vantage. Mr. ASHCROFT seconded the amendment. There was, he said, no more children in the institution to-Jay than there were .eighteen months or two years ago, and during the past two months Mr. and Mrs. Wright had had extra assistance. The joint salary of the master and matron was £125, but the house,coaLgas,andrations would bring the amount up to £2lO. Mr. BENT : Less the superannuation fee, it is not that amount.
Mr. Asncnorr conteqded that it would be unfair to the other foster-mothers to give Miss Dykes an advance.

Mr. FORSTIAM could hardlycall the proposed increase a material advance; it was simply an acknowledgement of the proficiency with which the school had been managed. Mr. HOUGHTON supported the minutes very heartily. He pointed out that Miss Dykes had a long period of service whereas the other foster-mothers were compara- tively new officers of the Board. If Mr. Thompson sent the minute back to the Committee it would pro- bably come before the Board again with the amount of the advance still further increased. _ .

- Mr. DAVIES expressed surprise at the opposition. He could well understand the opposition to the spending of £B,OOO or £lO,OOO for the extension of buildings, in face of the scandalously hich rates and the bad times, but he could not understand the opposition to the grant- ing of a paltry Lin increase to two valuaule officers i who had been n the employ of the Board nine years and had never received a single increase. Mr. HICKMAN said that if the committee felt they were not giving Mr. and Mrs. Wright the increase to which they were entitled he hoped the minute would be referred back and the amount raised. Rather than raise the aalary of one female officer and leave the others out in the cold to come cap-in-hand begging, be would advance the salaries all round. He supported the amendment in order that the matter might be fully discussed. . . . .

Mr. BENT said his original proposition was to ask for £1 each for Mr. and Mrs. Wright but he was assured by some influential members of the committee that £5 each would be satisfactory. He considered that a very modest sum, in fact he felt ashamed to be behind such a paltry request. Mr. Wright's predecessor received a salary of about £ll.B whereas Mr. Wright received only £B7 4s. less superannuation fee. Therewero sixty more children in the institution than when Mr. and. Mrs. Wright, were appointed. . Mr. JOLLEY said the matter had already been care- fully and thoroughly discussed. All the figures were laid before the Committee,. and what was now submit- ted was the deliberate decision of the Committeearrived at after careful consideration at a specially convened meeting. To refer the minute back without any instruc- tions would be a little absurd. Whatever might be said, it was clear from the tone of some of the speeches that the amendment could only be meant as a reflection on several officials. He (Mr. Jolley) objected to anything of the kind, and requested the Board to confirm the Com- mittee's action.

Mr. MATHER said the committee were unanimous in arriving at the recommendation and be hoped the Board would say they had done perfectly right. He asked Mr. Thompson to withdraw the amendment and let the increases be granted unanimously. TherO was nothing to be gained by referring the minute back as it would only come before the Board again. gr. THOMPSON said that so far as he was concerned, he had` no feeling against Mr. and Airs. Wright, but be was under the impression that several members of the Schools Committee were opposed to the increase. If the seconder would agree he would be pleased to with- draw the amendment, in view of what he had heard that morning. Mr. ASFICROFT would not consent to the withdrawal of the amendment and a vote was taken with the result that only Messrs. Hickman, Ashcroft, and Thompson voted for the amendment. The increases were therefore granted. Mr. HICKMAN said he would move•a further amend- ment that the Master's salary be increased' by £1 per annum. . . . .
-Tht-3.-OtERK You will have to give notice of that. Mr. IliciudAN said be would give notice. THE VAGRANCY PROBLEM: MORE ACCOMMODATION' WANTED.

At a meeting of the House Committee on June 29rd the proposal to impart practical fire drill and instruc- tion to the male °Ricers was adjourned for int-lair:v. The tender of Messrs. Smith and Walker, of Market Gate, for supply of gate porters uniform at an in- clusive sum of £5 17s. Gd. was accepted.—The Master directed attention to the continued overcrowding in the vagrant ward, and pointed out that, in consequence the detention system was almost broken down, the great majority having to be discharged the morning after their admission. It was received that theaction of the Master be approved, and that in view of the overcrowded state of the male vagrant ward, the Master be directed to discharge after one night's detention those vagrants i who n his °pluton, appear to be most deserving, but that he endeavoured to carry out the detention orders as far as was practicable. It was resolved to consider at the next meeting what steps should be adopted with reference to the painting and redecorating of the now hospital inside and out, it was stated that the Board and Committee room also needed attention. It was resolved to purchase 150 tons of firewood from Messrs. Davb., of Liverpool, at 18s. per ton carriage forward. With reference to the carriage on this quantity
it was suggested that possibly it could be brought cheaper by water than by rail, and it was left to Mr. Thompson and the Master to make what arrangements appeared most suitable.

At another meeting it was decided to grant a general leave to all classes of inmal es on Walking Day. The wages of Mrs. Langley and Mrs. Clements, attendants on female lunatics, were increased from 17s. 6d. to 20s. weekly. Mr. FORST-I,IW moved the confirmation of the minutes of the House Committee. Ile pointed out that the increases of salary to Mrs. Langley and Mrs. Clements were well deserved, as both attendants worked seven days per week and twelve hours each day. The Com- mittee had had to elax their rules in regard to vagrants, owing to the limited accommodation. He was afraid the question would force itself on the Board before long. The congestion was mainly in the male portion of the casual wards. There was accommodation in those quarters for 58, but they had to find room for an average of 70 each night. In winter the state of things was far worse—in fact he was told that the inmates of the casaal ward had to be packed like herrings in a barrel. The matter should he taken in hand with a view to providing better accommodation before winter.
Mr. THOMPSON seconded and said the vagrants ques- tion would have to be taken up by the House Committee. He hoped some good would come of the Commission which had been sitting.

Mr. BROOKS said some members of the Board might have received an erroneous impression. Mr. Forshaw said they had only beds for 59, but if they accoMmo- dated the inmates, every night they had really only room for an average attendance of 2-9. The minutes were approved. 'THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT THE HOUSE Mr. HICKMAN said he would like to know what had been done by Messrs. William and Ssigar Owen, archi- tects, with regard to the accommodation question. He understood that plans were to be submitted to the Local Government Board and their approval to the proposal utilization of the old infirmary asked for. , The CIIIIRMAN said the last information he received was that Messrs. Owen were preparing some pencil plans to present to the architects of the Local Govern- ment Board and that when the Board's assent to the alterations was given, they would submit the plans to the committee and prepare an estimate of the cost. He had not heard anything for the last tea or fourteen days, • Mr. FORSHAW : I think there is a feeling that we should like the improvement in this generation. (Laughter.) kt was decided that the Clerk should intimate to Messrs. Owen that the Board were anxious to heir from them on the subject. THE PROPOSED NEW SIDING. At the lost meeting the Board confirmed a resolution 'of a sub-committee that the proposal to erect a siding on the Cheshire Lines by adjoining the Workhouse be not entertained.

Mr. THOMPSON objected to the deo;sion having been come to at a poorly attended interim meeting and thought the full reasons for the committee's action should be stated. He moved that the sub-committee be requested to present a report to the House Committee on the matter.
Mr. %TOLLEY protested that such a course was out of order, but after discussion r. Thompson's proposal rn agreed to.

div.head: WOMEN LIBERALS' ANNUAL PICNIC.
div.p: WOMEN LIBERALS' ANNUAL PICNIC.
SUCCESSFUL OUTING TO BELLE VUE.

In the history of the Warrington Women's Liberal 'Association there have been many enjoyable outings, but this year's excursion, which took place on Monday to Belle Vue, will stand out as the most successful on record. The weather was all that could be desired, the arrangements were perfect, and not a single untoward incident marred the pleasure of the occasion. By dint of enthusiastic work on behalf of the Liberal cause, the Women's Liberal Association has earned the right to be regarded as one of the most valuable assets of the Progressive forces in 'Warrington. There ' is a good and steadily increasing membership, and the A.ssociation is always to the -fore in the successful engineering of bazaars or like projects which are occasionally required to keep up the sinews of war. To Monday's picnic the members were invited to bring their friends, and this was one of the occasions on which mere man IVai•welcomed.

Shortly after noon Arpley Station began to present an animated scene, far the trains for Longsight Station were due to leave at 12.40. From all parts of the town people hurried to swell, the waiting forces, and the total number journeying by the excursion would be about 1,200. Messrs. Crosfield's Prize Band, under the conductorship of Mr. E. Smith, accom- panied the trip and added considerably to the enjoy- ment by well played selections. Two special trains had been chartered and they were speedily filled. The tun to Longsig'ut was by no means' devoid of interest, for stretches of beautiful Cheshire 'country were passed e e route. Bathed in the brilliant sunshine, some of these picturesque spots were looking at their best and almost made one long to indulge in a rural ramble. In somewhat striking contrast, the hilly town of Stockport with its cotton mills next attracted attention. Longsight station, which adjoins Belle Vue, was reached in excellent time, and the trippers at once made their way to the famous Zoological Gardens to which the railway tickets secured free admission. The band, discoursing lively magic, headed the procession, and the multitude had soon taken possession of the grounds. To people in the Warrington district the attrac- tions of Belle Vue • are tao welllknown to need any detailed description here. Many of the excursionists who visited the resort for the first time were surprised and delighted at the succession of wonders unfolded to them. The fine collection of animals, ranging in variety from the rabbit to the elephant, V 7.1 S inspected with great interest, and there was a particularly Large muster to watch the feeding of the lions and tigers. The visitors were also able to gain an idea of how wild animals are trained,—young lions, leopards, wolves, and bears being put through a series of really wonderful performances in an open- air cage by trainers attached to Carl Hagenbeck's animal school. While some of the trippers easily con- trived tolose themselves in the bewildering "Maze," others underwent the realistic experience of a trip on the" ocean wave." One old lady, who appeared to take the " voyage " rather badly, was heard to declare that although she had fully intended to visit the Isle of Man this summer, no one would persuade her to go now ! The athletic grounds, shooting jungle, and boating on the lake provided plenty of recreation for the younger excursionists, and the time passed all too quickly. At five o'clock a capital knife and fork tea was served in one of the large rooms. A very cordial welcome was given to Mr. A. H. Crosfield who was ' unable to accompany the trip from Warrington but , followed by a later, train. The company also included Potts (National Reform Union), Alderman Tinnion, Mr. and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Clay, Mr. and Mrs. Edmund Osborne, the Rev. Herbert and Mrs. Dunnico, Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. William Roberts, Mr. and airs. W. Furness, Mr. Joseph Howes, Mr. A. H. Sanders, Mr. J. Elwell, Mr. J. Willet, and Mr. J. Howes, jun.. (registration agent). After tea there was a little speech-making, which will be found reported below.

During the evening those visitors who liked to " trip the light fantastic toe " conld do so to their hearts' content, a band playing an excellent selection of dance music. The crowning event ot the day, however; was the firework display. Seats had been reserved for the excursionists in the gallery, and they were able to view the spectacle to the best advantage. The scene presented was the memorable "Battle of Muliden," for which a special picture had been painted by Mr. R. Caney. A great number of men in costume were engaged in the production, and the horrors of the fight, resulting in the triumph of the brave Japanese warriors, were very vividly depicted. The wonderful display concluded, the excursionists had ample time to get to the, station from wiiich the first train was announced to start at 10.15. The journey was, however, somewhat delayed, and after a rather tedious ride Warrington was reached at 11.45. The second train followed shortly afterwards, and all the excursionists were agreed that the outing had been a most complete success In concluding a word of praise must be given to Mr. J. Howes. jun., who had charge of the arrangements on behalf of the Women's Liberal Association. THE SPEECH-MAKING , MR. A. IL CROSFIELD • AND THE TORY LACK OF POLICY.

After tea several short speeches were delivered, Mis- Potts,(National Reform Union) of Manchester, attends ing to address the gathering. Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes presided and expressed regret that their Presideat (Nlrs. Ziba Armitage) could not be with them. They were all pleased to see Mr. Crosfield, and she was sure the large gathering, must be extremely gratifying to him. ( Applause.) Miss Potts, in the course of a short address, said that as Liberals they were in a very cheerful frame of mind for they were on the eve of a great victory. She ,did not think there was any doubt about that at all—

the only doubt was what would be the size of the j victory—(applause)—and that was partly for her hearers I and for her to say. It depended to a certain extent on the amoust of good, honest, down right-work that the women did in their own constitu- encies as to what would be the Liberal majority when the time came. She knew they were all longing to have a chance to say what they thought. of the present Government. Although they would not have a chance to say it directly, she believed the women. of England would make themselves felt in the next. election perhaps as they had never done before. (Hear, hear.) She did not think there was any class of the community which had cause to thank the present. Government, and she was sure the women had less cause to thank it than any other section. If they thought of the increased price of the necessities of life due to the wasteful extravagance of the ministry of the past ten years, they would see that many results of that extravagance had fallen directly on the women of this country. Who was it that had to buy sugar for the household ?—the women, of course, and it was thanks to this Government that they all had to pay more for their sugar than they used to. They must do their best to put in a Government that would not raise prices, for it must beextramely difficult for many of them to make a shilling go as far as it. did ten years ago—in fact she did not think they could do it. The price of everything had gone up so much, not because there had been any reason for it, but merely because the money had been frittered, sqnandered, and thrown away in various directions. Take, for instance, the price of tea. We were at peace, and still the taxes on tea were kept up. If the women thought of that, when the time came they would put, more back into their political work than they had ever done before. (Applause). The cry had often been heard lately" Oh, for half an hour of Gladstone." She thought they all felt that. (Hear, hear.) They wanted a great man to rise up and say "These things shall not be. We will have a righteous, economical, and far-sighted Government." Still the spirit of Glad- stone was not dead. It never could die and it ived in her hearers and in her or it should do. It was for those who remembered these great ideals of peace, retrenchment, and reform, to see that the work did not die because one:greatleader had perished. They must take up the cause he left them and in every possible way forward those great principles for which he lived and in which he died. (Applause.) They had plenty of work to do in Wallington. They had a stiff 13;51it before them and they ought to earn the right to join in the shouting when the time came. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Crosfield had a very cordial reception ott rising to address the gathering. He said it had been his privilege to address a great many political gather- ings, but certainly he had never addressed such a pretty and attractive gathering as they had there. (Laughter i and applause.) It was delightful to see the ladies, : women and girls of Warrington taking an interest in. " ' politics and joining in that picnic, and he WRS so very I i glad that the weather was all that tbor could desire. iHe was sosry that the present Government was not as good as the weather. (Laughter.) The only thing that struck him as in common between the weather that after- noon and our extraordinary Government, was the fact that the Government like some of them at Belie Vise were having rather a warm time of it. (Laughter.) He was told that on that account, and as there were so rams attractiena at Belle VW:, thtlf. rlitieal remarks were to , lie Mt down to a few minntea Lko he would follow the , excellent example set by Mrs. Holmes and their visitor, IMiss Potts, whom they were so pleased to see present. (Applause.) They had a meeting in Warrington the other day in the open air and he then ventured to com- pare the political devices of the Premier to the clever soil Of Performances that one sAm LI"- a circus. (Laughter.) But Since that meeting it had occurred to him that there we're two comparisons that were nearer the mark still, arid one was the pictare'of a man who was learning to ride a bicycle. He dare say they had often seen the tinter. I tunate individual who tried to ride a bicycle and jerked first one way and then the other, and came a very sad cropper at the finish. (Laughter). But the very first time he (Mr. Crosfield) had the pleasure of speaking to his fellow townsmen and townswomen was in the old mission room at Bank Quay, and he was afraid he had a very bad attack of stage fight on that occasion. (Laughter). His duty that day was to recite a poem, about that strange animal called the chameleon. The story ran that two travellers in the deserts of Arabia had seen the animal at different times , and one said it was a beautiful blue colour and the I other declared that it was a beautiful green colour.They had quite an argument about it, and he (Mr. Crosfield) would read them what the poem said : So high at last the contest rose, From words they almost came to blows: When luckily came by a third ; To him the question they referred. And begged he'd tell them, if he knew, I Whether the thing was green or blue. 4 Sirs,' cries the umpire, 'cease your pother; The creature's neither one nor Cother. I caught the animal last night, And viewed it o'er by candlelight : • I marked it well : t'was black as jet. You stare, but, sirs I've got it yet, And can produce it.'—'Pray, sir, do ; I'll lay my life the thing is blue.' 'And 11l be sworn that when you've seen The reptile, you'll pronounce him green.' 'Well, then, at once to ease the doubt,' Replies the man, 'l'll turn him out ; And when before your eyes I've set him, If you don't find him black I'll at him.' He Enid ; and full before their sight Produced the beast, and lo I—ewes white. (Loud laughter). Continuing. Mr. Ceoseresp said be had seen many des- criptions of the Premier's policy or lack of policy on the fiscal question, hut he did not think the mystification that existed in the Conservative party exceeded the error under which those good travellers were labouring. (Laughter.) He would only say in addition that if they had no certain voice or leading from the man who was at the head of the Government, at all events there was no mistake about the policy at which a still stronger and more determined man was aiming, and the danger of that policy had been admir- ably alluded to by Miss Potts. They honestly felt that in the great political issue before them, especially in regard to Free Trade, that it was a qnes- Mon that vitalily concerned the women and children of Warrington quite as much as the men, and really even more than the men. Therefore it was not a ques- tion to be trifled with ; it was a very serious matter. The other questions that they had before them—whether It be education, or the clearing out of our too crowded centres, temperance reform, or even if it were a question of the proper and legitimate protection of trade unionism—which ever of those questions they considered concerned the mother of the family every bit as much as it did the bread- winner of the household. So they hoped that all present would take the advice that had been given by Miss Potts,and give the Liberal party a cordial and a really enthusiastic support in the best cause that a party ever had to fight for in politics. (Applause.) He had in conclusion very great pleasure in asking them to give a hearty welcome and a vote of thanks to Miss Potts for kindly coming to address them and at the same time to thank them all for so patiently giving him such a pleasant hearing. (Applause.) Mrs. Clay seconded, and said she hoped the members of the Association would carry out the advice so well given by Miss Potts. , The vote of thanks was heartily accorded. Mr. Joseph Howes delivered a short speech. The meeting, he said was a splendid one, and they bad enjoyed themselves at the tea table thanks to the bless- ings of cheap Free Trade food. (Applause.) They were present that day to demonstrate to all whom it might. concern that they meant to keep Free Trade food as long RS possible. (Applause.) In Warrington they would fight the next election primarily on the question of cheap food for the people, open ports for the workers, full interchange with all the world, and cheap sfood for the children, and in that they had to fight Balfour and Chamberlain. (Hear, hear.) Wherever the name of Crosfield appeared it meant cheap faod for the people. (Applause.) They were associating the name of Crosfield with Free Trade and" Crosfield and Free Trade" would be the motto upon their banners at the next election. Those banners were going straight to victory with a majority as large as the women by their influence chose to make it. (Applause.) The men were not present that day,but the men's masters were. (Loud laughter.) The Liberal party appealed for the homes, the children, and the lives of the people, and it was therefore in order that a demonstration like that should make up its mind on a question so important. They were fighting vigorously in Warrington ' • they would continue the fight till the votes were counted, and they knew what would happen then. (Loud applause). The gathering then dispersed.

NORTHERN UNION FOOTBALL The League Reconstruction Scheme. The annual general meeting of the Northern Rugby. Union League was hold at the Grosvenor Hotel, Man- chester, on Tuesday night, with Mr. Joseph Platt in the chair. The proposed reconstruction of the League as pre- sented by the committee was voted upon. The Scheme was that the present First and Second Division clubs should be combined in one league, and that the champion- ship should be decided on nearly the same principle as the county cricket championship, the honour going to the club with the highest percentage of points for matches played. Every club was represented save Millom. Pontefract, and Lancaster, and the resignation of the last-named club,now defunct,had been announced a few minutes before. Each delegate had come pre- pared to vote in accordance with the wishes of his club committee, and the settlement of the question did not take long. When the votes were counted it was found there were 18 clubs for the suggested change and eight against it. Thus the newproposals were again defeated. But shortly afterwards a motion was made and carried that in future a two-thirds majority should he sufficient to carry such an alteration. In this way there seems still a chance of the official scheme being adopted. It is open for a certain number of clubs to request a. flrther general meeting, and that is indeed what is likely to happen.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

WARRINGTON Bovs BIRCHED. At the Warrington Police Court Reeves Baxter (7), 16, David-street, and Walter Harris (0), 15„ Pierpoint- street, were charged with stealing a purse containing 1:39.6d. the property of Richard Mi telell, 12, Edgeworth- street.—The Chief Constable said it was rather extra- ordinary to bring boys of the defendants' age before the magistrates. In those cases he believed however, that it was in the interest of the lads that they should be prosecuted because there was is strong suspicion that they had not acted entirely without direction and training for older minds. On Saturday Mrs. Mitchell went to a neighbours house leaving the door of her own residence unfastened and leaving the purse on the rnantlepiece. She returned in a few minutes and to her surprise found the two defendants inside her house. On seeing Mrs. Mitchell the lads immediately went up to her ann asked for a bit of bread. She sent them away almost immedi- ately afterwards she missed her purse and reported the matter to the police, who discovered that the purse had been taken from the mantlepiece and thrown under the sofa. The brother of the defendant Baxter was before the court a week previously charged with stealing boots. —Mrs. Baxter said her son was being led astray by Harris.—Mr. Harris said his son was sometimes out until 12 o'clock at night.—The Chief Constable: Both lads have very doubtful home surroundings.—The magistrates ordered three strokes from the birch to be given to each of the defendants.

NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington police court on Monday, Samuel Jones, 5, Dale street, was summoned for neglecting his five children. Mr. Browne on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. stated that the defendant was a widower and was earn- ing 18s. per week, though be could earn more if he chose to do so. He would never engage a woman to look after the house, the work being left to a girl of 13. Defendant was constantly drinking and the children were in a dirty and neglected condition. Mr. Farrel, school attendance officer stated that Mr. Clarke headmaster of Sankey School had complained to him of having had to send the defendant's children home from school on account of their condition. He visited the house and found the children in a filthy condition. Defendant seemed to be absolutely indifferent.—Evidence was also given by P.C. Wood and Inspector Cox. of the N•S.PC.C. —Defendant, who promised to reform, was sei.t to gaol for three months with hard labour.

THEFTS OF CLOTHING. At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, before Alderman Hutchinson (presiding), Messrs. J. Rymer Young, A. Jackson Holmes, and W. Richardson, Annie Mather, 49, Hamilton-street, was brought up on remand from Monday charged with stealing from outside the shop door of Benedict Tyrer, at seven o'clock, on Satur- day evening, a youth's suit of clothes, value 12s. 6d. She was also charged with stealing from the same shop on June 10th, a pair of boots, value Ss. 6d., and further with stealing from outside the same shop at seven o'clock on May 27th, a youth's suit of clothes, value 15s. 6.- -Superintendent Monaghan said that on Saturday evening, the prisoner went into the prosecutor's shop and selected a pair of men's boots and paid Bd. on them and they were laid by for her. She left the shop and was seen standing outside, and shortly afterwards a suit of clothes was missed. The matter was reported to the police, and the clothes were found pledged Ist Buckley's pawnshop. The Superintendent went to the prisoner's house and said that he wanted her on suspicion of steal- ing the clothes. She replied, "Oh, dear, it is the drink." On being charged at the Police Station she replied "I did take them." On June 10th the prisoner went into Tyrer's pawnshop and after leaving a pair of boots were missed from inside the shop. They had been pledged for the prisoner by a girl named Holmes at Mather's pawnshop, Pinner's-brow, for 6s. 6d. On May 27th, the prisoner again went into Tyrer's shop and paid 2d. on a pair of boots. A suit of clothes, value 15s. 64., was missed after she had left. Inquiries were made and a number of pawntickets were found in the prisoner's house. The vest had been pledged at Mather's pawn- shop, and the coat and trousers at Tunstall's Winwick- street. When charged prisoner replied "I did take them. It is drink that has done it." Her husband gave her good money nearly every week. She had five children, and one was only five weeks old.—Mr. Mather said that he expected his wife had been drinking with other friends. He bad not been at work full time for some weeks, but his wife had not been destitute. She had never stolen anything before. The Chairman said the case was a most serious one, but the Bench had decided to take a lenient view of it. Prisoner would be fined 20s. in the first case and a conviction recorded a the other two cases.

CIIASTENING OF DELILAII,
GERDA. GRASS (Author of " ii Urnrcrofes Son," ite.).

in the molitude of a little room, fitted up is a study and suggesting pathetically enough a hard struggle between poverty and artistic taste, a young woman of a Jewish cast of beauty sat tapping away as for dear life at a type-writer of the poorer sort. And all day long, as her thin, small fingers fluttered, like bewildered white butterflies, over the keys, the everlasting click, click. click of the machine, varied only by the regularly recurring tinkle of it+ little bell, had been irritating the supersensitive ears of her landlady, old Martha Stock, who, mice in Delilalis somewhat palmier days of lively and innocent childhood, had been the servant of the Paseenha family and had since, by dint of care- ful hoarding and stern closefistednetem, lifted herself into an independency that she might well have called snug, hail her crabbed and discon- tented nature ever permitted the sue of such a cheery-sounding adjective. There was a brief interval of blessed peace when she brought in the meagre meal and, setting it down with her wonted taciturnity before her young lodger, re- ceived a fleeting smile from the sombre, pool- black eyes from which the fire and radiance that she remembered well, though with no stir of feeling in her chill, uninotherly heart, had died out long ego, even as the peachy bloom had faded from the thinning cheeks. "You have found a customer for Garcon, I hope, Murtha ?" said the girl, 88 she pipped her tasteless tea end stoically repressed a tired sigh. " I do 80 hate to have to sell him, but—needs must when the devil drives, you know. It will soon be the thirty-first of December, and I need all the money I shall get this month for myself. I am almost out at elbows. Alas !" a gleam of counterfeit mirth lit up her eyes, " I can't, like Garcon, wear ono coat all my life." She stooped and petted with her painfully thin hand a sufficiently well-fed looking poodle curled up in the folds of her skirts. Then she fell to "I have found a buyer, Miss Delilah. He would give five guineas, he said, seeing it come of a good breed, and I struck the bargain at that. For the dog's an old beast, thinke I, and its best days is over. Knocking off the five shillings you promised me, that makes five pound precise. I got the money straight off, but the gentleman thought you might want to say goodbye to the dcg in your own way, he says, so lie leaves it with you till six or seven to-night, and then he sends at messenger for it. Here's the money, Miss Bentonite,. And very welcome I should think it'll be. For money's a power. in the land, but what anyone ever could eels in dumb animals I never could think. I can't abear them, myself." " No, I suppose not," returned Delilah, and her black eyes fixed themselves Turiously on the hard, wrinkled fire before her. " I suppose not. We have queer notions, some of us, you see. Well, you can take the things away now, Martha. I've had sufficient, thank you. When the bell rings to-night I'll take Garcon into the kitchen and you must manage the rent, yourself, please. I don't want to be near when lie's taken. By the way," she said, stopping the old woman as she turned to leave the room, " I hope any banjo-tummiug in the evenings has not dis- turbed you, Martha ?" " I'm not a great lover of any kind of instru- ment," she made answer in her toneless way, " but one gets used to everything, and, once you're used to a thing, you're better with it than' without it. You've no call to mind me, I'm sure." "Thank you. You see, one feels so gay and light of heart when one's finished with this tire- some old machine," said Delilah, with a low, little laugh. " And it's a sachheart that never rejoices." " Did you sleep all right last night, then, Mites Delilah ?' asked Martha at the door—for cour- tesy's sake, not that the answer was of interest in the least. " Thank you, yes, But I had to take lauda- num, of course, as usual. And it's a nasty habit to get into, and makes you feel heavy and dazed next day. Besides, you have to keep on increasing the dose, you know." " Wm, Wm," said Marlin, and adding—again for courteey's sake—a wrinkle of concern to the rest, she took herself out of the room with her tray. Then the monotonous tapping began again. Time table was littered with MSS.,—fashion articles, stories for mediocre journals, boudoir gossip and so forth—not one of them a thing that an author of self-respect could look upon with glow of pride and thrill of pleasure. And the machine itself held in its grip a pessimistic short story destined to find its home in the columne of a provincial weekly. " The soul," it clicked out harshly, " is but a sort of perfume clinging to the human clay," and then time bell gave out a tinkle like a mirth- less little laugh, " and there are humane born without souls, as there are flowers born without fragrance, and the Almigimty. responsible for the one as fur the other, can have uo just preference for either,—" Then the dusk come, and the tired eyes drooped and Delilah Pasetudia pushed aside the machine to make room for her elbows, and, folding her arms upon the tumble, bowed her throbbing head upon them, and bye and bye fell feet asleep. Outside, the snowflakes were damming wildly, like a host of mad witches in white, and a mourn- ful wind whined through the keyhole and the cracks of the door and 80011 rattled mildly at the cesement. A pallid, lialf-dead ember dropped with a rattle into the grate, and Delilah, once known as Delilah the Dashing, awoke with a start and shivered. It lied grown cold and dark. Shaking off Garcon front her dress, she rose and fed the famished fire with an unusually lavish hand, put the poker between the bars end watched the yellow flames dart in and out of the dark caverns. Sat so for a long, long while, musing, till the coals began to glow and rugged pictures grew out of the black and the red. Then she took the head of time persistently pawing dog between her bands and looked into his plaintive eyes. " Yes," she said, "it is good-bye, old boy. Good-bye for good and all I Not for the sake of a worn-out jacket—as if that could part US when never the pangs of hunger could —but just for time sake of a worn-out heart. Worn-out hopes. Worn-out ambitions. To-night I take iny leap into the dark. That's why we can afford a good, brave fire. Did you wonder at any ex- tratvagance, maybe ?. Yes, it's good-bye, Grii.rcon,

Site saw the bright little nest of EL study she bad made his refuge from grief and care, and where she had told him all her plans mid her dreams and read out to him her latest piece of work, and they two had laughed and cried together over the comedies, mid tragedies of her mimic world. She saw the gay, Bohemian little circle where, by virtue of her sudden liana-clasp with Success, she bad reigned as queen, and where the had won a lover in Geoff Morrie, the artist, poor brit of promise then, rich and famous now. Here in quaintly-pretty, but inexpensive costume fash- ioned by herself, she had been elected pleasure. maker to them all, dancing the Serpentine dance or some pirouette of her own invention, singing plantation songs with banjo accompaniment, gravely, and with glowing cigarette impressively uplifted, telling fortunes to awe-stricken groups' of her own sex, or putting her faithful com- panion, Gareofi., through a progromme of :mins. lug tricks. Through the merry throng at Youth's high carnival, she had carried with dancing step and laughing eye many a hidden sorrow, many a bitter disappointment. For one swallow maketh not a summer, literary failures had crowded one upon the heels of the other and many a grief was gnawing at her heart. The pictures of the Past grew darker. Clouds had come upon love's fair sky. For site was proud, with a firm belief that a woman should be cold, and he was hot. blooded and somewhat dis- trustful of her airy colpiettings. Also, lie did not quite like the cigarette between her lips mid the blue fog of scented smoke about her girlish head. But the final estrangement cone when he took ex- ception to her intimacy with the notorious Madame %%idea, who, divorced from her husband for reasons aufficient, but having beauty, wit and wealth, lind yet found friends enough to help Let into positien again. ", it is impossible that you can respect and like this woman, Delilah," he maid. " She is good for • copy ! ' " Delilah answered lightly, puffing it long streak of smoke towards him teasingly. " She is any model for the oen- tral figure of my next romance !" " I am serious, dear," he said. " Let the romance go hang ! Be a woman first and a writer afterwards: And a woman should be, above all, sincere !" The words stung her to the quick and a hot Such rose to her cheeks. " I hope," she answered icily, "I do not need a man to teach me how to be a woman. You have found so many objections to me of late, Geoff, that I think you had better look elsewhere for your ideal. I cannot climb the high pedestal." " Delilah, you don't love me," he cried, "if yea can turn from me like that !" " Pray let us say no more about it," she re- turned with a careless smile, twisting the cigar- ette in cruel fingers. , For a long while lie stood looking at her silent- ly. Then he said, simply, "You will give me, however, the sittings you promised me for that picture of yourself for the Academy ?" "I do not break my promises," she answered, in trouble-free tones. "I am ready for you at any time." "Thank If it is a success I shall be glad to owo it to you, and I wile send you smaller copy of it fcr your study as a reminder of my gratitude. And when you look upon it, Delilah, remember this : I need no other ideal than you—that inner self you hide so carefully from us all—Heaven alone knows why ; 'tis pride, I suppose l—but which, nevertheless, I have caught many glimpses of in your eyes, your voice, your work." At a word from her he would have come back; without. it. nn I Ho had loved her as a man, not as a slave.

PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.'

"I am just thinking how I can encourage my boy to cut out a name for himself." "Give him a sharp knife and a school desk." "WHY do they call it the piano= forte'?" "Oh, I suppose so many people bombard it so unmercifully." MINISTER: "IS your father at home, Wil- liam?" William: "Yes; but he's got rheumh- tism so bad he ain't safe to talk to.' "Musx Igo to school again, mother?" Of course, dear." "Why, mother, I heard you tell father last night that I knew a lot too much." "THE funny-bone is in the elbow, isn't it, pa?" Father: "Yes, my son." "Well, pa, is that what makes people laugls in their sleeves?" "JorriveY, did you take your cough medicine regularly in school. as I told you?" "No'm ; Tommy Budds liked it au' he gimme an apple for it.' "You see, boys," saki a teacher, "that two and two always maka four, and nothing else." "Oh, yes, they do," cried one youngster; "they sometimes make twenty-two." "I'm sure I don't know," cried the father, "I really don't knew what to do with you, Henry. Is there anything good in you?" "I think so," replied Henry. "I've just eaten a piece of mince pie." "WHAT do you mean by 'preponderance of evideeee'?" asked the teacher. The reply was: "Pre,' before, and • ponderance' from to ponder, so that it is evidence previously pondered." ELDERLY GENT: "I am eighty years old; RI7 lad, and I don't ever recollect telling a lie. ' Cheeky Youth: '"Well, you can't expect your memory to reliable at that age." BROWN: "I thought you were a vegetarian, but I hear you eat mutton." Robinson: "I am not a bigoted vegetarian. I only eat the meat of siich animals as live on vegetable food." Misritzss : "Jane, have you broken another plate?" Servant : "Yes, mum; I did it on pur- pose. I'd smashed thirteen, you know, and that's sich an unlucky number." MRS WALLINGTON : "This house is as Cold 1111 a barn. I wish you would do something to make it warmer." Mr. Wallington: "Certainly." And then lie accommodatingly lighted a match. "DO you think it's true that every man has his price?" asked the heiress. "I'm sure I don't know," he answered thoughtfully ; "but if you want a bargain, you needn't look any further." "I'LL fight the boy who did that," said a lad, "if he weighs a ton." "Well I did it," said one of his hearers, "why don't you begin?" First Boy (after seeing who it was): "You don't weigh a ton." AN illiterate matron wrote to ask a well-known headmaster when it Would be possible for her to "inter" her son. The headmaster promptly and politely wrote, "Dear madam, I shall be ..,very glad to undertake your son at once." OLD GENTLEMAN : "How old are you. my little man?" Newsboy: "Nearly seven, sir.' Old Gentleman: "And how long have you been in the newspaper business?" Newsboy: "Oh, ever since I was a kid." "WHY, Johnnie, what has made your cheek swell up so?" "The master cuffed me." "But von look as if you were actually pleased owl. it." T'Oh, he sprained his wrist doing it, and had to dismiss the school r. BRIDE (exchanging bridal costume,for travel- ling dress): "Did I appear nervous at all during the ceremony, Clara?" Bridesmaid (envious): "A little at first, dear; but not after George had Eiaid I will!'" Mns. EARGANE : "Haven't you got the tooth- ache, John?' Mr. Bargane : "No, in- dear; why?" Mrs. Bargane : "on, lam so sorry that you have not. I bought a new toothache cure to-day, and I wanted you to try it." MABEL : "Whose picture is that on your mantelpiece, Jack?" Jack (with confusion): "Er—that's my sister. She's married, and lives in Australia." Mabel (calnily): "Sister by birth or by rejection?" "I BELIEVE you'd stand before a mirror all day," said Mr. -Closely snappishly, "doing noth- ing but changing your dresses." "Perhaps I- would," replied Mrs. Closely dreamily, "if I had the dresses." "ALLow me to lay this little gift at your feet." "No, no ;I never take any presents from my gentleman friends." "But this is only a copy of my poems." "Oh, in that case, I don't mind. .1 thought it was something of value." 4 MAGISTRATE: "And wiat did the prisoner say when you told him you would have him arrested?' Complainant:. "He answered mechanically, your honour." Magistrate: "Explain." Complain- ant : "He hit me on the head with a hammer." "MOTHER, what are twins?" asked . little Bobbie. "I know," chimed in Dolly. "Twins is two babies just the same age; three babies is triplets; four is quadrupeds; and five is centi- pedes." "Loox here," said one young hopeful to an- other. "That knife I had from you won't cut a bit. You told me when I bought it off you for twopence that if I once had it I would not part with it for Is." "Well, you won't" was the en- couraging reply. "WHAT is it, dear?" asked his wife 4 passing her cool hand over his troubled brow; "what is on your mind?" "Nothing," answered the poet, mournfully, gazing at the blank sheet of paper before him; 'nothing, I can assure you." 'Dom% John had been set to work in the kitchen garden. After a while he paused in his task, hinting suggestively to his father, "The fish are biting like fun in the river." "Well, sobnie," replied the father, reassuringly. ,"you keep on hoeing potatoes, and they won't bite you!" MOTHER: "Did you have a Pleasant evening at Auntie Bell's party?" Kitty: "Delightful, mamma. Everything was so pleasant, and Mr. James told me I was as pretty as a picture." Mother: "You must not listen to flatterers, Kittie." Kittie (very thoughtfully): "I know it isn't sensible; but, mamma dear, how shall I kv"-v they flatter, unless I listen to them?" MR. JENKINSON : "I've been out half the day trying to collect money, and I'm savage enough to break the furniture. It beats everything how some men will put off and put off. A man who owes money and %Won't pay it isn't fit to asso- ciate—" Servant (opening the door): "The butcher, sir, is downstairs with his bill." Mr. Jenkinson : "Telrhim to call again." "Now, Mr. Peck," said Mr. Spudds to his grocer, "you must not try to persuade me that this Java coffee really came from Java, because I know better." "I would not try to deceive you, air," replied Mr. Peck, "and I will add that even our Vienna bread did not come from Austria." WIFE (standing with her;husband before shop- window) : "Here are so many things that would give pleasure to your wife, and that you might purchase for her • but, no matter however many beautiful things ;here are, you seem quite indif- ferent, as though you saw nothing." Husband: sure proof of my affection for you, for love is blind." Dn. WINES, principal of a boys' school, one day had occasion to cane a boy, and it is to be supposed did the work very thoroughly. The lad took his revenge in a way that the doctor himself could not help laughing at. Dr. Wines's front door bore a plate on which was the one word "Wines." The boy wrote an addition in big letters so that the inscription ran, "Wines and other lickers." AN old laily hppeared recently at a school in a poor district to complain of stone-throwing by one of the boys. She was requested by the master to look at the lads and to point out the culprit. The old lady took a careful look round, but failed to identify the lad. "I don't see him at present," she remarked, adding with the air of one who had been made the victim of a plot. "I think—l think he must have had his face washed." MAMMA: "What is Willie crying s about?" Bridget: "Sure, ma'am, he wanted to go across the street, to Tommy Green's." ' Mamma: "Well, why didn't you let him go?" Bridget: "They were havin' charades, he said, ma'am, and I wasn't sure as he'd had 'em yet." "So you are learning to spell, are you, Johnny?'" asked the youthful student's grand- mother. "Yes, grandma," was the reply. "Well," said she, "let Inc hear you spell bread." "I &on% believe I can, grandma," replied the little fellow, "but,l think if I had a small piece of cake I could spell that."

A HORSE STORY.

A remarkable incident is reported from Penang. A horse put his tongue out at his stable companion through a hole In the side of the stall. The other animal bit the tongue, and so seriously that the stricken horse had to be shot.

div.head: Width of Roadster Tyres.
div.p: The Width of Roadster Tyres.

For fast riding on the road a new size of tyre is this season being affected by many riders, the Width being 1,1 inches, the tyres being of the open- sided variety, and the tread specially thickened on the back cover. The ,idea of making a differ- ence between the thickness of the tread on the back tyre seems to be a good one, for it is generally agreed that at least 75 per cent. of punctures occur to the back tyre, the front tyre of a bicycle as a rule being much more free from puncture troubles than the rear wheel.

div.head: Is Touring on the Decline ?
div.p: Is Touring on the Decline ?

The opinion has been expressed in more than one quarter that cycle touring is no longer as popular in England as it was when there Were fewer Cyclists. In support of this view it is urged that tourists are rarely met at home or abroad, and that the membership total of the Cyclists' Touring Club compares unfavourably with the figures of former Years. It is admitted that the cyclist is more übiquitous than ever, and that the bicycle is pressed daily into every possible utilitarian service—but this is not touring. Probably years of public familiarity with what was once regarded as a curious and novel mode of travel has shorn the tour of its charm to adventurous spirits. Then the reduction of railway rates has undoubtedly encouraged cyclists to betake themselves and their steeds by rail to districts which they can explore awheel in comfort from a holiday base, without the burden of luggage. Yet these riders make no show aS tourists The fact is the pioneers of the cycling Pastime were composed of hardy athletes who delighted in piling up mileage and battling with headwinds and gradients, while to-day vast numbers of quite ordinary persons, of both sexes, use the Cycle as a means of pleasure travel witheut ever Claiming or winning recognition as tourists.

It will, how- ever, probably be years before these become the "vogue, and in the meantime, the Eadie, G. & H., and New Departure Coaster Hubs, the Fagan Two- Speed Hub, and the Hub Two-Speed Gear, all seen to be growing in favoiir and use.

The Cost and Condition of our Roads; 10 consequence of disquieting statements as to The deterioration of our main highways, due to Motor traffic, the National Cyclists' Union recently circularised the‘ surveyors of the county, councils throughout the 1 country. The replies received show (1) that there has been an increase in the cost of road maintenance in recent years; (2) that in a large majority of cases surveyors are of opinion that the motor-car traffic has had an injurious effect on road-surfaces; and (3) that tar macadam, 80 far as it has been tried, has proved successful ia minimising the dust nuisance and making a piore satisfactory and durable road-surface.

div.p: SUMMER SHOWERS,

The light Atacintosh cape or poncho, costing only two or three shillings, should be a portion of every cyclist's outfit, for even if you do not ride in it you cant by ensure really efficient protection when sheltering bora a summer shower beneath a friendly tree or hedge.

div.head: What a Bicycle will Bear.
div.p: What a Bicycle will Bear.

The strength and durability of the bicycle are bothing short of amazing. In poor neighbourhoods a, common spectacle is two hooligans careering along on an aged crock, one supported on the step. xin the music-hall stage, in the hands of skilled Performers, in the evolutions of cycle polo teams, or "Oder the strenuous propulsion of the news-carriers Who cycle through the dense traffic of the London atreets, we are confronted daily with the weight- bearing Power of the common cycle. A girder Ira • me has lately been tested under a load of 27 cwt. ▪ fore giving way, This weight is equal to that of ighteen average men. Short of collision or tnarnolation beneath waggon-wheels, bow seldom ureaksdown occur Actual fracture of the frame tor forks rarely occurs to even old bicycles. A rider tceanae aware of a grating noise on his machine 'which baffled location. After riding 15(1 rnf,es lie Ilisooverecl the souud to proceed from a fractured fork blade. The bicycle, though eight years old, 'as high grade, and the existence of a liner in the Lork side probably averted a serious accident:

div.head: SIMPLE SPRING-MAKING DEVICE.
div.p: SIMPLE SPRING-MAKING DEVICE.

The .Engineering Review describes a simple device for making springs, which may be useful to amateurs. it consists of a hole drilled through a bar of Bessemer steel and a pin bay- ing a wheel head entering it. A second hole, perpendicular to the first, admits the metal, for example, wire, to the nin, round which it i coiled by turning s tho wheel head.
DANGERS OF IMPROPER ELECTRICAL
TREATMENT.

Electricity, although of great value as a remedial agent, may in the hands of an inexperienced or careless operator do a great deal of mischief, says Science Siftings. Blindness has been caused by an improper application of the continuous current to the face; fainting, pasm% hysterical fits, and palsies have been induced by the administration of powerful shocks; and fresh apoplectic attacks have incurred to patients who had previously suffered from cerebral hemorrhage. Such accidents are only to' be avoided by thoughtfulness, physiological knowledge, and medical experience. So, beware of electrical quacks!

div.head: INSTINCTS OF INSECTS.
div.p: INSTINCTS OF INSECTS.

How is it that ephemeral insects, which only live a few days or weeks, and have no parental education, acquire their instincts? M. Perier explains it by supposing that in geological ages, like tho carboniferous era, when insects flourished, there was perpetual summer, owing to the greater size of the sun, and insects had time to acquire instincts, which they have trans- mitted to their descendants now. The seasons came into force, he thinks, in the Tertiary epoch, and brought a shorter life to many in- sects, which, however, retained their inherited instincts.

div.head: THEORIES ABOUT RADIUM.
div.p: THEORIES ABOUT RADIUM.

Contemporary science, like the outside of a coral reef, is in a state of growth or change, and one experimenter, or theorist, may refute another, hence reports of progress are some- times contradictory. Becquerel holds that tho radium emanation consists of fragments of atoms which have lost positive 10119, and the ions them- selves, but according to the recent experiments of Professor M'Clelland, the emanation consists neither of one nor the other. The emanation, in fact, does not carry an electrical charge, and the same conclusion has been arrived at by Pro- fessor Patelli, using a different form of apgara- tus. This is not the only recent observation that seems to tell against the accepted views about radium.

div.head: "NEW" THEORY 1.,400 YEARS OLD.
div.p: A "NEW" THEORY 1.,400 YEARS OLD.

For a long time we have prided ourselves that the mosquito-malaria theory was quite a modern one, but it now turns out to be 1,400 years old, Sir H. Arthur Blake has told the Royal Asiatic Society that a communication from the Secretary of the Ceylon Native Medical Association, mentioning that in old books the mosquito was described as one of the means of propagating malarial fever, had so struck him that he made further inquiries and found that in the medical works of Caraka Susruta and other ancient Cingalese Writers it was men- tioned that there were sixty-seven kinds of mosquitoes, and further that there were four kinds of malarial fever caused by the bite of those mosquitoes. At present about thirty-six to forty species had been named in Ceylon, so that, as a matter of fact, recent discoveries were only re- discoveries. The books he referred to were written In the sixth century; therefore, they had only re-discovered what was on record 1,400 years ago.

div.head: EARTH'S HEAT CAUSED BY RADIUM.
div.p: EARTH'S HEAT CAUSED BY RADIUM.

Professor E. Rutherford suggested some time ago that the new element, radium, may possibly he considered as a source if not the source of heat from within the earth. He states that since one gramme of radium emits enough heat each hour to raise 100 grammes of water through ldeg C., a simple calcu- lation shows that the present loss of heat from the earth is equivalent to that supplied by the presence of shout 20,000,000 tons of radium. This amount may seem very large compared with the small quantities of radium hitherto separated, but is small, for example, compared with the annual out- put of coal for the world. It can be readily deduced that this amount of radium if distributed throughout the earth's crust. corresponds to only five parts in one hundred million million per unit mass. This is a very small quantity, and calcula- tions based on the observations of Elster and Geitel show that the radio-activity observed in soils corresponds to the presence of about this pro- portion of radium.

div.head: FORMATION OF PEAT ROCS.
div.p: FORMATION OF PEAT ROCS.

An interesting description of the the formation of the great peat bogs is given by Professor Weiss. lie shows hew bogs originate in a hollow place in which water collects. In the water the spores of the bog moss germinate' and gradually the moss chokes up the pit, just as various water-plants choke up ponds. The bog moss bunches itself together and rises above the surface of the water. On this soft, spongy bog ' moss plants like the insectivorous sundew flourish. As the moss grows dead vegetable matter accumulates on the bottom of the hollow, and after it has accumulated to a certain extent, instead of decaying completely anii becoming soil, the decay is arrested owing to the presence of the large quantity of water. That is the beginning of the *formation of peat. Peat is found in two forms—an upper layer of fibrous peat which is dry in the summer, and below that a layer of soft moist peat. In many cases the peat-bed spreads beyond its original hollow and encroaches on the surrounding vegetation, which it kills by excluding the air. Often forests are killed and submerged by this means, as in some parts of Germany, where in low-lying districts forests have been eaten away by the peat- bog.

div.head: SOMETHING ABOUT WATER.
div.p: SOMETHING ABOUT WATER.

Water exists in three different states; as a solid in ice; as a liquid in water; as a gas in vapour. To cause it to pass from one of these states to the next following' one heat is neces- sary. Dig a hole in the ice of a Swiss glacier i in summer, and place a thermometer n the hole; it will stand at 32deg. Farcnheit. Dip your thermometer into one of the glacier streams; it will still mark 32deg. Tho water is therefore as cold as the ice. }fence the whole of the heat poured by the sun on the glacier, and which has been absorbed by the glacier is expended by simply liquefying the ice, and not in rendering either ice or water a single degree warmer. Expose water to a fire; it becomes hotter for a time. It boils, and from that moment it ceases to get hotter. After it has be- gun to boil, all the heat communicated by the fire is carried sway by the steam, though the steam itself is not the least fraction of a degree hotter than the water. In fact, simply to liquef, ice a large quantity of heat is necessary,. and to vapouriso water a still larger quantity is nocers• eau.

div.head: CURIOSITIES OT "MOULD."
div.p: CURIOSITIES OT "MOULD."

Speaking at the Royal Institution on "Fungi," Professor Ward said that tho mould on wall paper was rather on the paste than on the paper. With cheese, it was the water in it that gave rise to mouldiness, while that on boots .was an outcome of thcr blacking, not the leather Ninety to ninety-five per cent. of fungi was water, and this was so in the case of mushrooms. There was a popular mistaken notion that these fungi were nutritious; but there was very little nutriment even in a hundredweight. The other fivis or ten per cent, was made up of nitrogen oxygen. Jollies in particular were the choice food of moulds. Some fungi were so luminoun that. photographs had been taken of them by their own 'light. The fungi were very destruc- tive. They simply ate up whatever they fastened on, mostly wood. There was also a mould which the Profesror called "lurking fiung,." TReso generally attacked grain and in a way went to sleep between the seed and its husk. They were voisonols. and had caused epidemics in tne past. It was nis miler mat ben-ben i was caused solely by a "lurking fungi" in the rice. This was a very serious thing to Eastern nations, especially to an army in the field. . THE SMALLEST MiCROBE SEEN.

The emalle-st object yet recognised under the microscope is the bacillus of.pleuro=pneumonia in cattle. :'.Chi s is one-tenth of a micron—or about 1-250,000 of an inch—in size, and still smaller microbes, as yet unseen, are supposed to be associated with smallpox, hydrophebia, and the horse sickness of South Africa.
