div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

"Vaccinated Veal." Sir,—ln view of the letter on this subject, which appeared in your last week's issue I should be glad if you would allow me to draw attention to the practice followed on the Continent in regard to the disposal of vaccinated calves. The following particulars are taken from the Report on the preparation and storage of calf lymph which was submitted to the Local Government Board by Dr. Thorne Thorne in 1897 :—Paris.—After use the cakes are sold to a butcher at a loss of from 30 to 40 francs each. Berlin.—After collection of lymph, the calves are sold to the Jewish Rabbi to be slaughtered for food. We were informed that a larger price is given for them than is ordinarily the case with calves brought to the Central Meat Market. owing to the fact that they are in such fine condition as the result of good feeding while at the Station. Dresden.—The calves are obtained by a local cattle dealer, who charges 20 marks for their use, and who removes them for slaughter immediately after collection of the lymph. Cologne.—Che lymph is collected from the calves after they have been slaughtered and the carcases are then sold on the next day. Genesa.—After vaccination and collection of the lymph the calves are sold tea butcher at a loss of about £1 on each calf. It is difficult to imagine anything mere revolting than the practices revealed in t`fe foregoing extracts, unless it is the practice of taking the diseased cowpox matter (miscalled pure calf-lymph) from these beasts, and injecting it direct into the pure blood streuu in the insane attenapt to reap health by sowing disease. It would require the pen of a Swift to adequately deal with such a colossal abstirdity.—Yours etc., J. P. S. 27th June, 1305.

The Swiss Militia. Sir,—l have received the enclosed letter from Professor Raget of Geneva, in amplification of his lecture at Appleton Hall on June 17th. As I think this may be of interest to a gool many of your readers I should be much obliged if you would insert it.—Yours etc.,

GEORGE R. CROSPIELD. " The Swiss militia is a fit subject for consideration in the country because there exists a certain analogy and real likeness between the public mind of Britain and the public feeling of the Swiss. In both countries everything points to a desire that the civil body may be paramount : that nothing may conduce tea militaris- ing of the commonwealth. The difference between training to the use of arms, as in Switzerland, and the Volunteer principle relied upon in England consists in this, that the Swiss have felt that to safeguard the liberties of the subject or citizen, it is incumbent on everyone to sacrifice a certain measure of their personal ease ire order to provide a military force for the safety of the nation. A training which does not mean a uniform military instruction for the healthy young manhood of the country; which stops short of supplying the country with the necessary organisation for war and does not systematise the latent military energies of the people into a visible fighting force—such an imperfect effort marks out a nation as lagging behind others in the struggle for life. fully worked out system' of citizen training is essential to the well-being of a nation. Its advantages may be styled as reaching far beyond its immediate purpose. They have a wide social and educa- tional value. Everybody learns something in the large school of military discipline,and from his own military achievements, however modest they be. Through the military training of the civilian, every quality is disseminated that is essential to a sound business-like life. Such a national militia must however, not be confused with conscription : it is simply an improvement upon voluntary effort in military matters. As a means of drawing from a nation its best, be it technical, moral or intel- lectual, without any waste of quality, without entering into competition with any legitimate civil requirements, the Swiss national militia system hits the mark. At the age of nineteen every Swiss is called upon to appear before a medical military board, and these officers "ear-mark " those who are fit to undergo the hardships of training. These do not pay the military tax. Their instructional period does not extend beyond the first year, and lasts only a few weeks (from seven to twelve weeks) ; later, and so long as their liability lasts, they meet periodically in the regimental unit to which they have been posted. Every one begins as a pri rate soldier, there is no exception whatever. The distinctive feature of the Swiss militia is that it claims in every respect to be an army, except in one : it does not contain a single " regular" or professional soldier, though it is tnobiliried and monceuvres always under service, or war con- ditions."

Are the Liberals a Progressive Party? Sir,—ln your issue of June 2lth, there is an account of an open-air political meeting held the previous Wednesday evening.and a lengthy report is given of Mr. A. H. Crosfield's speech delivered at that assembly. The taxation of Land Values, the Housing Question, and Temperance Reform were all mentioned by Warrington's prnapective parliamentary candidate, who evidently believes that the Liberal party, if returned to power, will seriously attempt to efficiently solve these burning social problems. As a working man I am deeply interested in political questions,but I have little admiration for the Liberal party, whose leaders (with a few honourable exceptions) appear to me no less re-actionary than the average Tory member. _ _

----- Crosfield speaking of the Prime Minister remarked that" as a man who danced on the tight rope, as a juggler or a conjuror, he beat anybody at a circus "and further stated that many members of the cabinet simply bad to dance as the Premier told them. 1 contend that the support given to Mr. Balfour is exceptionally mild compared with the idolatrous worship of Mr. Gladstone, by the large majority of the Liberal party, during the time he was the acknowledged leader of Liberalism. I also wish to remind Nit.. Crosfield that the Liberal party during their last term of office 1892-5 made no serious attempt to pass any of the items con- tained in the fainous vote-catching Newcastle pro- gramme (1591), which had been superseded by Lord Roseberry's "clean slate." and a revival of the old stock platitudes of Free Trade (so-called). Liberalism Tefused in 1393 to do anything for the unemployed and a large majority of the Liberal members absented them- selves from the recent debate on the Government's un- employed Dill. The Liberals supported the granting of a pension of Rl,OOO per annum to the retir- ing speaker Mr. Gully, but evince little prac- tical sympathy for the aged and infirm poor of the great industrial classes, who are stigmatised as paupers and disfrarchised for receiving in the form of parish relief a miserable weekly .pittance of six or seven shillings. Many of the prominent Liberals are quite as efficient as even Mr. Balfour at "political con- %ring, jugglery or tight rope dancing"—for example Lord Roseberry on the Home Rule question and Mr. Winston Churchill. who, although now an advocate of Liberalism, is indebted to Conservative support for his seat in the presentlParliament. Liberalism is, to my mind, simply Anti-Toryism, and if the electorate of ^his country hope by returning the Liberals .to power they will thus secure any great social or industrial teforms, they will, I fear be doomed to bitter dis- -rppointment. By the way, is there any real nuidamental difference
in the political principlea of ti a Progressive Labour League and the average branch of the orthodox Liberal party? An early ans,ver will obliga.—Yours "DEMOCRAT."

div.head: Religious Instruction. Rev. H. Dannlca's Reply to Csnon Stevenson.
div.p: Religious Instruction. Rev. H. Dannlca's Reply to Csnon Stevenson.

Sir.—Absence from home prevented me replying to Canon Stevenson's letter last week, but with your per- mission I will de so now. Let rue, however,. repeat what I stated in my sermon that your correspondent is much more tolerant and broad-minded than the majority of the Anglican clergymen. Of course I assume now what I have no desire to doubt-that Canon Stevenson is prepared to recognize Free Churchmen as brethren end fellow members of the Church of Jesus Christ. Patron- age is one thing, justice is another; the former we scorn theilatter sooner or later we mean to have. i Now there is not much in Mr. Stevenson's letter I ' need deal with because the whole of my contentions are admittedly correct. Still before I deal with several points of importance it may be wise to do what is commonly called "mark time." In the first place the i National Society was founded in 1811 and not in 180 i as stated by him. Secondly building grants were I made up to 1883 and not 1870. Thirdly The state I recognised its duty and allocated a sum of money for educational work 18-1 years prior to the date given by Mr. Stevenson. Whether these mistakes are immaterial or not is a matter of opinion; that they are mistakes is la matter of fact. Now with regard to the S.P.C.K. and its work, I still i maintain that the work of that Society had no connec- tion whatever with a system of elementary education as 1 we understand that term to-day. Their schools were.es I Mr. Stevenson states, charity schools pure and simple. 1 They. were all closed against Nonconformists. I accept 1 Mr. Stevenson's figures. but ask in return, what was a I paltry 500 schols for a Church of the whole aristocracy and which received five million yeerly from tithes ? I content myself with this brief reference to the work of the S.P.C.E., because it is altogether outside the present controversy. If Mr. Stevenson does not share this opinion. then lam quite willing to discuss the matter in detail. Tee misappropriation of vast Slims of money: the closing of all charity schools, Grammar Schools and Universities against the children of Nonconformists; the infamous Schism Act which provided no public or private school master could teach without making a declaration to con forin to the liturgy of the Anglican Church and obtaining a license from the Bishop ; the imprisonment of Nonconformist for teaching their town children &-c., will provide materials for a few letters. One thing is quite certain that this clerical monopoly of the means of *education reealted in such ! general ignorance, brutality and debasement of manners ! that it would be di:licult to find a parallel in the whole I of English history to the gaeen Anne and George I. I periods. The next point of interest is this : WAS the National Society formed to cake over the growing work of the S.P.C.N., or was it from alarm at the spread of the system started by Joseph Lancaster, the estimable Southworth Quaker ? Mr. Stevenson contends that it Iwas formed for the former reason and " that unless I can offer proof to the contrary he must maintain the accuracy of his contention." Well, if Mr. Stevenson honoured me by reading my sermon as reported in your columns. I think he could hardly have omitted to read the Quotation I gave from a letter written by the first Earl Russel, who was, by the way, a staunch Churchman and not a passive resister. Earl Russel says "The Established Church pronounced az first the opinion that the children of tht: poor shoal not go to school at all But finding that George TIT, had eepressed a wish that every child in his dominions should be taught to read and that national opinion was favourable to education. changed its grouad and in 1811 set up the so-called National Society on a narrow and exclusive principle." Again, 'The clergy were in those days— even the liberal clergy—opposed to the education of the poor but finding that the cause of education made progress they agreed in 1811 'to set up a society for founding and maintaining schools." Dr. Bell who was in reality the founder of the National Society was himself opposed to the poor being taught ,I either to read or cipher because it would tend to make ' the labouring classes discontented with their lot. contend that no unbiassed men can really study all the available evidence cennected with the establishment of the National Society without coming to the conclusion that the main objects for which the society was founded were first to check the 'progress of the Lan- castrian movement started in 1793 and next to control popular education in the interests of the Established Church. I pass over for the preeeat the cost of the scheels .cc. and simply repeat that this vestion is a national one not a local one and that an ooinioa i 3 of little value in a discussion of this sort. Whet we require is some- thing more reliable. I dealt with this point very fully in my sermon and Mr. Stevenson has not pointed out any inaccuracy. Until he does sot can justified in assum- ing that he admits that the Anglicans have no more claimito special consideration than Free-Churchmen have So far as Mr. Boucher's case is concerned, lam sorry that I cannot accept Mr. Stevenson's interpretation of same. Your correspondent admits the accuracy of the quotation given, and condemns the language, but says that had I known the circumstances I weuld not have. referred to it : (1) Because the book has never been I used in any college ; (2) because the writer was asked to send in his resienetion, the Committee dis- approvinr of his teaching; (3) because the book was published some years after his resignation. In reply to those assertions I beg to that although the book in its present form was published after Mr. Boucher's resignation an earlier edition of the book was printed ten or twelve years previously and circulated among the students. Moreover the one point on which Mr. Boucher (after 30 years of teaching) had to resign was, according, to the Bishop of Bangor, " that he "taueht that Dissenters' baptism wee invalid cal this is not Catholic doctrine." His general teaching was dis- cussed at a meeting of the clergy at Bangor, the Bishop being in the chair. and Archdeacon Williams amid the applause of the clergy said that Mr. Boucher did tech , in a crude way • but these wore the principles of the Church." The Vicar of Bethesda also contended that " Mr. Boucher hail done a giant's work for the Church." To put the matter in a nut- shell Mr. Boucher taught that Dissent is sin and in doing so he had the support of English Church Canons, the "Church Times" and the English Church Union with its 4,000 clergymen all of the sem;-Rornenisine type. At the present time fonr officials of Church Training Colleges and a dozen diocesan inspectors are members of the English Church Union—a Union seeking corporate reunion with the Church of Rome. Supposing Mr. Boucher had been Vicar of one of the 8009 parishes in this country where there is no day school other than the Anglican. Supposing that he had had the power( as 10,000 have) to nominate the founda- tion managers and had chosen 33 he watild have chosen men of his own particular school of thought, who would have celled upon him to resign ? I maintain that Mr. Boucher's teaching is a fair tyne of teal teaching given in hundreds of schools throughout the country, and an prepared to produce evidence in support of this contention. This is the kind of teaching that is repugnant to our most m•ofound convictions, and when we are forced to pay for this,is it any wonder that we protest? I have already trespassed too far on your space, and will deal with several points touched upon by Mr. Stevenson in a future issue. Ira !conclusion let Ttle again gay I appreciate the courtesy and kindly spirit of Mr. Stevenson's letter and am very sorry that we are compelled to stand on opposing platforms. This conflict, however, is not as is often alleged a battle between sects contending for supremacy. The Free Churchman claims his right RS a citizen and in no other capacity. In other words he seeks to place the schools supported and maintained by the people under the control of the people. We ask nothing for ourselves save onrrights as citizens.We can accept from the State no help to teach our own special belief much less a preference.and we cansubmit to no Parliamentary enactments which place us at a disadvantage for the same reason. Let the various sects teach their own children what they like but it must be at their own cost and assuredly not at ours.—Yours sincerely
lIEII3ERT DUNNICO.

div.head: PRIMA-DONNA'S HUSBAND.
div.p: THE PRIMA-DONNA'S HUSBAND.

One day I discovered that Paris boasts of an institution unique in its way—"an academy for prima-donnas' husbands "1 (writes Frances Keyzer. in "The King.") I Someone had given me the address of a former actor, who, I was told, could supply me with some profes- sional information concetning these people. It was in an apartment on the second floor, a few minutes from the Conservatoire. The man was out, and I awaited his return. The office lead into a spacious room, and through the open door I beheld a puzzling sight. A gentleman, faultlessly dressed, a gardenia in his button- hole, waS on his knees depositing in a basket-trunk a quantity of ladies' wearing apparel, carefully folded up and placed within his reach. Near him a cross-looking elderly woman was carefully watching him. All at once the woman called out, "Ca n'est pas cela ; vous faites des pHs. Recommencez ! " and, with an impatient gesture. emptied the contents of the trunk on the floor. I heard something that sounded like a suppressed oath, ancf the victim started refolding the clothes and repacking them. At that moment my friend, the ex-actor, returned. " Who is that man in the other room," I asked, " and what on earth is be doing ?" He first closed the door, and then said He is Madame P.'s fiarare. The lady in the other room is my assistant, and, at Madame's request, he is being taught many useful things. When he knows how to fold and pack dresses, I go into the question of con- tracts, and show him how to deal with tricky impresaries and theatrical managers. I have made a special study of this. Have I had many pupils? Yes, I have had of few, and they pay me exceedingly well. I am afraid however, that Madame P. will have a little trouble with the man she is going to marry. He is intelligent, but very awkward with his fingers, and a prima-donna's hus- band does not require brains. He must be handy.,

of which would interest itself in some particular branch of the society's work, He was glad to hear what the Chairman said in regard to the smoke. question because t ley knew that, in a town like War- rington, the smoke, like the poor, would always be with them. (Laughter.) There was not in the thoughts of the promoters of the society the slightest wish for one single moment to make themselves objectionable or to take up the work in any spirit of opposition. There were firms in the town—of which he believed the chair- man's was one—whose members and managers had given ' "re it attention to the smoke question, and the society ought to feel most grateful to them for having grappled with the problem and, to a certain extent, succeeded in solving it. The great value of the society, or his opinion, lay in the kindling of a public spirit. What they wanted to achieve was that every person in the town should wish to see it beautiful and not wish to be destructive, careless or negligent. When once they had cultivated that spirit, he felt sure that the difficul- ties would melt away. Another advantage was that it was a society in which every person in the town could unite. Here the Conservative lion could lie down with the Radical 1 unb—(laughter)—and the Anglican wolf would not annoy the Nonconformist sheep. (Renewed laughter). Here they would all beat one, and anything which brought them together and promoted among them the spirit of unity and goodwill, was in itself a thing to be prized. (Applause). Mr. HENRY ROBERTS seconded. As one of those individu as who specially possessed the characteristics of the Liberal lanab—(laughter)—he had very great pleasure in following the Conservative lion who had so eloquently discoured to them on that important topic. The speeches had fully supplied the necessaryarguments for a society which had for its object the improvement of the general conditions of life in this town. First acd foremost, one had to face the terrible fact, which upon reflection carried with it an enormous amount of sadness, that 75 per cent, of the population of this kingdom lived at the present time in towns. As one of those who grew up to considerably past early manhood born and bred and reared in the town itself, he cold, appreciate the desires that most men had,which werejbe- gotten of a passionate love of the country to sea occasionally something brighter than the black smoke which came from Monday morning to Saturday at noon from so tuany of our chinmeys.Whan one further remem- bered that, no matter what might be done in regard to tramway services which were one of the greatest boons ever brought to municipalities as they enabled so many of the working class population to breathe the fresh air and see the beautiful sights of the country, in spite of that for some generations at any rate, a very large. proportion of the working population must perforce live in more or less close proximity to the works which found them employment. It therefore became a very serious duty that all those who had leisure and ability and the keen desire to do something for those who were not so sa.tisfacto,ily placed, socially and financially as they themselves were, should help to make the conditions of life a little better than they were at the present time. One very important point was the effect on municipalities which the cultivation of public opinion would have. He knew how difficult it was to carry out a groat improvement when there was a united and interested opposition. determined as far as possible that it should not be carried out. It was perfectly true that the public opinion of Warrington had been in the main in favour of improvements which had been effected, but unfortun- ately it had not been organized and concentrated,and to some extent the Corporation had suffered from the want of the support which a society of that kind was so well able to give and to cultivate. The.y had around Warrington some of the most beautiful outskirts that any town could possess. It appeared to him that that society could do a great deal to help, by bringing influence to bear on public opinion outside Warrington, to preserve the rural characteristics of those outskirts which, unfortunately, through our rapidly increasing population were so quickly diseppearing. Many evils which unfortunately existed in consequence of dense crowding of houses in small areas were only in a lesser degree being rapidly repeated in the outskirts of the town. That was one of the things in which we could learn an important lesson from our continental neighbours. He wished we had the powers that muni- cipalities in some countries on the Continent possessed. by which they were able, by securing certain control over land which was unbuiltupon,to prevent evils which wore such a socit.l danger. He was convinced that that society could become a source of considerable improve- ment in more ways than he could possibly describe. The resolution wee carried una-Arnously. THE CONSTITUTION OF THE SOCIETY.

Alderman BENNETT moved : " (a) That any person who is interested in all or any if these objects shall be eligible for membership on payment of a minimum annual subscription of one shilling. (b) That the officers of the society shall consist of a president, vice- presidents, treasurer and secretary, and shall be elected at the annual meeting. (c) That the committee shall consist of 12 members, three to be nominated annually by the 'Warrington Society, and the remainder elected at the annual meeting. The president, treasurer and secretary shall be ex-officio members of the colunittee." He said it was a source of unadultered pleasure to him to assist in the inception of a sociery such as thia, as he had been trying for a considerable number of years to inculcate the gospel that utility and beauty should go band-in-hand, and that commerce might be coupled with artistic taste and beauty. (Hear, hear.) In start- ing this society they were making another step forward —and they had made many steps in the right direction in Warrington of late years, It was desirable to have the power of existing agencies increased by the creation of healthy outside opinion. They hoped to get a large amount of sympathy from the workingmen and also to receive valuable essistance in their work from the fair sex. In every department of municipal life it was quite possible that with a littlo care and con- sideration rind a common spirit of co-operation they might achieve much better and brighter results. Mr. C. E. PARKER seconded, and said there was no one more anxious than he was to see the town made beautiful. Unless the smoke nuisance was abated, all their efforts would be to some extent neutralized. As a manufacturer who had cured his own smoke he might have a feeling of superiority and look with some disdain at other manufacturers who were spoiling the town by their smoke. (Laughter.) The society wanted to get the co-operation of the manufacturers and interest them in this smoke question. It was a very difficult question —more difficult than many imagined, especially in cer- tain trades, but he trusted that the society would use their influence with manufacturers to gain their assist- ance. div.head: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON.
div.p: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON.
FORMATION OF A NEW SOCIETY "To Increase the Beauty of the Town
and Preserve Features-of Interest."

A Beautiful Warrington Society is tile latest addition to the institutions or our town and its object is to promote nay measures calculated to increase the beauty of the town, and to preserve from neglect or , destruction all features of interest in it. The minimum annual subscription is one shilling, so that the means of membership are placed within the reach of all. The society was formed at a large and representative meeting held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon and presided over by Mr. F. Monks. Mr. John Fairhurst, who has acted as hon. secretary of the movement from its in- ception. was present, and the principal speaker was Mrs. Higgs, the founder of the Beautiful Oldham Society, • The CHAIRMAN said he must confess that one was rather amused at the idea of a Beautiful Warrington Society, because Warrington was not considered a very beautiful place, although he believed its surroundings were as beautiful as might be found almost anywhere in the country. Before introducing Mrs. Higgs he had only one word to say by way of caution. He had heard from time to time what he called very rabid speeches about the selfishnes of manufacturers, and it was said that it was all owing to such selfishness that we had so much black- s-noke in Warrington, and that it ought to be altered. He did not think there was anyone more alive to the desirability of con- coming their own smoke than the manufacwrers— even from a selfish point of view—because he thought they reaiized that if they could succeed in consuming their own smoke in such a form as would ! be practicable,„ they would be able to save at least one half of their coal bill. Firms like Pearson and Knowles, • Monks, Hall and Co., Whitecross, and one or two others consumed a very large quantity of coal,and he thought they might be left to solve the problem as far as they could, realizing that it would be a profitable operation to them. Mr. FAIRHURST then announced the receipt of a number of apelogies for nen-attendance. Lady Greenall had wired stating that Sir Gilbert and herself were unable to be present, but hoped that the meeting would , be successful.

The Rev. WILFRED J. STANTON wrote that he was very glad to learn that it w3a proposed to start a society in tVarrington for promoting the beauty of the town, and preserving its features of interest. He was sure that much more might be done in our largo towns in this direction than was attempted at present, and that if they were rendered more healthy and pleasing, some of oar great soc:al problems would be on the way towards solution.

Mr. ROBERT PIZRPOINT, M.P., wrote stating that it would be impossibe for either Mrs. Pierpoint or him- self to attend the meeting, as he must be present in Parliament, but he would read in the Warrington papers the result of the meeting. Mr. WILLIAM LONG wrote that he had bean unfortu- nately called to London, or it would have given him pleasure to attend and to help in any way he could to further such laudable objects as the members had in view for the beautification of Warrington and the dis- trict. He thought it was a most desirable movement and though perhaps too long delayed, one would fain hope that a good and lasting work might yet be done for the benefit of those who were to come after them.

Letters expressing willingness to support the move- ment were received from Mr. John Lee, Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Mr. George Dolan, Rev. James Davies, and Mr. L. W. Reynolds. Mrs. HIGGS who was cordially received, said she felt under a decided difficulty in coming to speak from beautiful Oldham to finbeeutiful Warrington—(laughter) —because she considered that if she were to bring a number of Oldham people to Warrington on a picnic they would probably say that Warrington was already more beautiful than Oldham. (Hear, hear.) Not only that, but the difficulties which they had to con- tend with in Oldham in the way of making the town beautiful were such that it was really in the ,! nature of an heroic enterprise to set to work to grow anything in Oldham at all. But had they not I always found that the very difficulty of things made , people embrace them? In reply to any criticisms of the proposed title of the society—such as, for instance, that it would excite mockery—they could say that they had a history and that at one time both Warrington and Oldhern were beautiful. Mrs. Higgs proceeded to trace the foundation and growth of the beautiful Oldham Society. She pointed out that much good was being done in the immediate neighbourhood by I having an annual tree planting day on which the inhabitants wore encouraged to plant trees. Not only had the beautiful Oldham Society accomplished something in their own town, but it was also firing people with an ideal, and they had had letters in proof that that ideal was needed, from the far away places of England. Many things they wanted to do could not be dons by private effort and the great thing MAS to have by the side of such bodies as the Town Councils, Education Ceinraittees, and different societies connected with places of worship, some society that would be a kind of repository of:the ideals of the many. What the Oldham Society had succeeded in accomplish- ing far beyond her utmost dreams was to plant an ideal in the minds of the eeople and the beauty of the Society was that, beginning with a very few enthusiasts, the idea had so taken hold of the minds of the people that it seemed, as she watched its growth,' something like a tree itself. In connection with the Society they had an Information Committee which I gleaned knowledge of what was required to be done in I various:parts of the town.By the efforts of the Society a , certain slum district had:been'chenged as if by magic,the I owners getting to be ashamed of unsightly property. Trees had been planted and 'gardening was encouraged. They were on the eve of forming a Young Beautiful Oldham Society, and they were going to get the children to sign a pledge in which they promised not to destroy plants and trees, or pluck wild flowers by the roots, not to destroy birds' nests, and that once every year they would try to sow seeds somewhere in Oldham or the neighbourhood. They were hoping to hare the co-operation of all the teachers, eel the children would be enrolled members at one penny each. The movement was, to her mind, one that, was the most likely to be fruitful. Already many children had been encour- aged to grow bulbs and the exhibits at the annual show had trebled in three years. Dealing with the smoke nuisanees,Mrs.'Higgs referred to the MC. ces iful efforts made in Oldham to encourage enthusiasm amongst the men employed as fire beaters, with the object of abating the nuisance. She made extensive inquiries and found that a great many apparatuses were very unsatisfactory and that, after all, a good fire beater wes the best smoke preventer they could get. The real crux of the whole matter was that they wanted to give,as they did in Americe,some inducement to make the fire-beaters feel public-spirited enough to keep down the smoke outputiff they got that,they would better the state of things for masters and men, and it would be for the good of the whole town. They wanted com- mittees to be grouped all over the town to report as to improvements which could be made. Mrs. Higgs con- cluded an interesting address with an appeal to her hearers to do their utmost to mike the town really beautiful. (Aoplause.) The Cu.\ IRMA.N said he was sure they would all be quite willing to see Warrington changed as quickly as Oldham haebeen. In asking the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson to move a resolution, Mr. Monks migrate- lated 1 the rev, gentleman on the honour which had been conferred upon him. (Applause.) The Rev. Canon MORLEY STEVENSON moved:—" That in the opinion of this meeting it is desirable to form a society with the object of promoting any measures calculated to increase this beauty of the town and. to preserve from neglect or destruction all features of interest in it, and that the society be called the Beauti- ful Warringtou Society." He said he felt it was a great honour to have the privilege of moving the resolution, because he had faith enough to believe that the move- ment had within it the springs of life and of perman- ence. Shortly before coming to the Town Hall he met one of their chief townsmen and asked him if he was coming to the meeting. The reply was "Certainly not" and the gentleman added "I think anybody who has got to your age and deliberately starts a new society and adds to the number of societies already in existence ought to have twelve months with hard labour." (Laughter.) Canon Stevenson proceeded to relate how he became interested in the movement. On reading an article on "Beautiful Oldham " he thought that some- thing of the kind might be achieved in Warrington so he got into communication with Mrs.Higgs and obtained a great deal of useful informantion from her. It occurred to him that there was one man in Warrington who would not throw Cold water on the movement so he went to his good friend Alderman Bennett and told him that he thought the subject was something in his lino (Laughter.) Alderman Bennett did not throw cold water on it, but he pointed out that there already existed in Warrington the Warrington Society and that one of its objects was very much the object of the Beautiful Warrington Society. The authorities of the Warrington Society were approached and they said they would have no feeling of jealousy whatever if a new society strove to carry out the work, because although it was one of their own objects, it happened that the work of the Society lay mere in other directions. All kinds of titles were reaggested,—most of them savoured either of some connection with the rates or with what were commonly called mutual im- provement societies. (Laughter.) The more they came to reflect on " Beautiful Warrington," the more they felt it was a title which had certain merits of its own. He ventured to think that Mrs. Higgs had started a work which would spread through the length and breadth of the country, and that there would he many towns which would rejoice in putting the adjec- tive " beautiful " before their names. The society had no intention whatever of interferiug in the slightest degree with the work of the Town Council. After all the Town Council was a body which was largely influ- enced by public opinion, and the object of the society would be to mould that opinion to desire that the town should be beautified. The society would be worked largely by a series of small sub-committees, each

W. Lee occasioned them some uneasiness by reversing the balance of points, defeating S. Holbrook 15-9, and thereby giving his side the lead. W. Roughley made a good attempt to reverse the situation and after opening badly against J• Hewitt be peeled at 14 losing the odd points. It was left to W. Butterworth to reduce the Pearson and Knowles lead by defeating J. Boyle 14-14. F. Miller placed a different complexion upon the game by defeating J.Holbrook 15-3. Whatever visions of victory had been entertained by the Pearson and Knowles men they were immediately dispelled another game going against them and their opponents regaining the lead which they held after th 3 first game.

Pearson and Knowles did not however, give up the game without a struggle and A. Bill showed that defeat was by no means assured carrying his score against G. Monks to 15-13. Dawson followed in a match with J. Shaw and proved his teams' undoing losing 15-6. The remaining games all went in favour of Rylands' who ran out winners by 37 points.

The match between Corporation and Rylands' Netting was followed with interest as the representatives of Warrington's august body could rightly be described as an unknown quantity this being their first season in connection Ivith the competition. They did not make by any means a promising start the first game leaving them 9 points in arrears. W. Monks, however improved the situation and after his game with J. Mather four points separated the teams.

The Rylands lead was next wrested from them,though a game later they recovered their position, which they improved immediately, R. Savory defeating J. Powis 1542. The outlook of the Corporation team at this period was far from rosy, but four wins in succession placed them in a safe position, and the points in the concluding three games being divided, the Corporation team won by 27 points.
No more matches will he played until Saturday week, when farther progress will be made in connection with the second round.

The Bulls Head team still maintain their position at the lead of the Warrington and District League table with 5 games won out of six played,and it is evident that ' they will take some moving from their position. Fearnhead however 'mean to run them very closely and by defeating the Horse and Jockey team on Satur- day they further improved their position. They were however considerably off form as a victory. of 17 on their own green cannot be considered as a particularly brilliant performance. The game was not without exciting incidents as with nine men off the green the totals stood at 112-100 in favour of the home team. J. Smith improved matters from the point of view of the home team by proving far too good for A. Shelmerdine who lost 3-15. C. Roberts added to the uncertainty of the game by only scoring Bto his opponents 15, and when W. Bowering • and T. Harrison took the green Harrison required to win by 12 point to give his side the victory. He failed , most signally being himself defeated and Fearnhead : were saved the mortification of being defeated at home. --- cannot understand the poor display which the Cemetery men have given this season. Last year they carried everything before them and their visits to foreign greens wore anticipated with some apprehension by the teams which entertained them. This year they ! have shown a considerable falling off and while they are still a team which is not to be treated lightly, their name is not "bogey," which it was last year.

Last Saturday they were entertained on Sankey green and were defeated by 45 points. The most surprising game was the one between J. Jackson and G. Ball, jun. Ball has throughout the season done fairly well but he received a most thorough beating, only placing two points to his credit.

Sankey can now be considered fairly in the running for the championship, and it will be a severe struggle between them and the Fearnhead team for the second place, as there is little likelihood of either of the con- binations improving upon the record of the present leaders.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

Warrington have yet to record their first victory of the season, for the Liverpool and District League match with Everton at the Corporation baths on Tuesday resulted in the,defeat of the home team by five goals to one. There was a large attendance to witness the encounter, Everton having a very good reputation as exponents of the game.slr. Snowden,of Liverpool ,was the referee.ln the first half Warrington were outplayed, and Morris, the well-known Everton custodian, was very rarely called upon to save. Skinner quickly opened the Everton scoring account, and although Woods did good work in goal, Gommersall added a second befor: the interval. In the second half three additional goals were registered for the visitors by Hayes,Forruby and Sharrocks. There was some excit- ing play and eventually Charles Ashton sent in the only successful shot for Warrington.

The second team made a very creditable show against South Hill and had hard lines in being defeated by five goals to four. The game was very keenly fought throughout. South Hill were the first to score through Haddon, but Turner quickly equalized. Rathbone was warmly applauded for the smart way in which he came to the rescue and cleared when Barker was in difficulties in goal. Pemberton next scored for Warrington in fine style, but the visitors again got on the attack and two more goals were placed to their credit by Turnbull and Haresnape. The opening of the second half was marked by a splendid effort on the part of Turner which resulted in that player scoring. White and Turnbull sent in successful shots for South Hill and Pemberton added another for Warrington.

div.head: £lOO,OOO FOR LABOUR COLONIES.
div.p: £lOO,OOO FOR LABOUR COLONIES.

- , The Rev. W. Carlile, founder of the Church Army, announces th:tt a scheme has been formulated for the expenditure of £lOO,OOO in establishing five labour colonies in different portions of the United Kingdom for the employment and accommodation of 300 men in each colony.

We are asked to state that owing to the very great demand for the Bovril Bonns Picture "The Little Lady Bountiful "by Fred. Morgan, there will he a slight delay in the delivery of the picture% The scheme closes on the 30th inst., and all coupons must reach the office of the company by. thati data. All possible expe- dition will be used, and it s hoped that all pictures will be delivered before the end of July.

The above results reflect great credit upon the teachers and students at the Technical Institute and at the Evening Continuation Schools. The list in the case of the Technical Institute includes four distinctions as com- pared with two last year. We would draw particular attention to the position attained by Mr. Stanley C. liatbbotie in advanced bookkeeping, he having obtained the first place is the examination with 118 marks out of a maximum of 120, and also to Mr. Arthur Keenan, who obtained the third place in the Spanish examination.

Oue feature of the examination which must be satisfactory to the town is the success of those students who are employed in the Public Offices. Mr. S. C. Rathhone, to whom refer- ence has already been made, together with four other students, are on the staff of the Borough Treasurer; two of the four obtained first class certificates, and the other two obtained second class certificates. Of the students employed in the office of the Director of Education who sat for tbePe examinations two obtained first class certificates. Whilst making these remarks there is no Intention on our part to detract from the good work done by the other students, the results being in many cases most meritorious. The names of a large number of the students who obtained scholarships to the Technical Institute from the Evening Con- tinuation Schools will be found amongst the successful candidates.

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT -COUNCIL. The fornightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there, were present—Messrs. S. Woodward (presiding), G. Pilling, C. Roylance, H. Eyes, G. Egerton Warburton, T. Baxter, H. M. Davies' ' J. H. Davies 41. Smith, T. Wright, S. Woodward, W. Harrison, T. Antwis' J. Spruce, J. flutter, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, .1. B. Chad- wick, A. G. Guest, Admiral Jones Parry G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. B. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector), end Dr. Adams (medical officer). MOTORISTS AND THE MAINTENANCE OF THE ROADS. The Clerk said the Council were invited to piss a similar resolution to that of the Bucklow Council who considered that the increased cost of the up-keeps of the highways and police supervision should be provided by taxation up n motor cars with other than iron tires and be fixed according to horse power and not according to weight and that the fines on offenders against the Act should he considerably increased and the proceeds together with that from taxation divided among County Councils according to mileage of main roads. Mr. Swinton pointed out that District Council roads were affected to an equal extent by the motor cars. It was decided to suppose the action of the Bucklow Council. C.T.C. NOTICE BOARDS. The Clerk stated that the secretary of the Cyclists Touring Club wrote regretting that the Council could not see their way to accept the responsibility for the up-keep of the warning boards in the district and as the Council of the C.T.C. was not prepared to continue to bear the expense single handed instructions had been given for the plates and posts to be taken down. Mr. Baxter: The removing of them does not need to trouble us. Mr. Pilling: You do not ride a bike. Mr. Baxter: lam always careful when I am coming to a hill. Mr. Wright: Motor ears go so fast that the drivers cannot see the warning boards. Nothing as done in regard to the matter. COUNTY' COUNCIL EXPENDITURE. The Clerk intimated that the Clerk of the Northwich Urban Connell had written stating that the replies to his letter on the subject of County Council expenditnre were with one exception in favour of a conference being held. Representatives were invited to a conference at the Crewe Arms Hotel, on Monday, July 3rd, when resolutions will be adopted for submission to the County Council. At the conference the dust nuisance caused by motor traffic would also be considered. ovERSEERS OUTSTANDING ACCOUNTS. Mr. Wright reported that the calls upon the overseers of Acton Grange, Alvanley, Frodsham Lordship, Keck- wick, and Ashton Grange, had not been met. The Clerk was instructed to write to the overseers asking for the immediate settlement of the calls.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Bowling. Saturday's matches in connection with the second round of competition for the Finlayson Cup attracted a large crowd of spectators to the King and Queen Hotel green, and some excellent trundling was wit- nessed. The match between Kylands (No. 1) and Pearson and Knowles (No. 2) teams had the expected result the first-named combination qualifying for the third round rather easily. An excellent start was made by them as the first game gave them an advantage of ten points, though the next game saw their lead re- duced to almost vanishing point.
